news.content_original: https://ukhsa.blog.gov.uk/2026/11/05/uk-providing-specialist-care-to-aid-worker-with-ebola/ This post relates to an emerging incident and will be updated as new information becomes available . A British person has been diagnosed with Ebola after helping with the outbreak response in the DRC and has been brought to the UK for specialist treatment. They have been safely transported back to the UK via medevac - a specialist flight during which an individual receives detailed medical care, and are now in one of the UK's High Consequence Infectious Disease (HCID) units at the Royal Free Hospital, London. HCID units are specialist NHS units designed to safely treat people diagnosed with rare and serious infections. Large infectious disease outbreaks like the current Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) require a large scale, international response. Specialists from countries around the world are assisting on the ground in DRC. Outbreak responses like this one always carry risk of the infection spreading to those who are responding. The risk to the UK public remains low. The UK has well-established systems, specialist facilities and highly trained staff for managing infectious diseases like Ebola. This post explains what is happening, how Ebola spreads and what you need to do. Why is this person being medically evacuated and why can’t they remain in DRC for treatment? The medical evacuation of a British worker with a high consequence infectious disease such as Ebola is to ensure that the individual has access to specialist care within the UK health system, while being closer to family and other support networks during treatment and recovery. This approach reflects the UK's commitment to supporting humanitarian workers who undertake difficult and important work on behalf of vulnerable communities around the world. Due to the precautions taken, this medical evacuation will not increase the risk to the UK public. Do I need to take any extra precautions? No. The overall risk to the UK has not changed, and the patient is being treated in isolation. You do not need to take any extra precautions. How is the specialist unit at the Royal Free Hospital different from an ordinary hospital ward? The Royal Free Hospital has specialist high-level isolation beds and some of the best facilities in the world for treating unusual infectious diseases. The patient is being treated in isolation. This means there is minimal risk of Ebola spreading as a result of this case. Staff in these units are highly trained and follow strict protocols to protect themselves, other NHS staff and the public. Can Ebola spread to other people during a medevac transfer to the UK? This is extremely unlikely. The patient was transported by highly trained specialists who wear full personal protective equipment (PPE) and follow strict infection control procedures throughout the journey. How does Ebola spread? Ebola spreads through direct contact with the body fluids of a person who is sick with the virus, such as vomit, diarrhoea or blood. It is not airborne, so it cannot be caught from particles in the air. This makes it very different from infections such as flu and COVID-19, which spread much more easily through coughs and sneezes. Healthcare workers caring for patients with Ebola wear full protective equipment when they are in close contact with a patient. This prevents the infection spreading by creating a barrier between the healthcare worker and the bodily fluids of an infected person. What are the symptoms of Ebola, and how long do they take to appear? Symptoms can appear between 2 and 21 days after coming into contact with the infection, and on average after 8 to 10 days. Illness usually starts suddenly with a fever, headache, tiredness, muscle pain and a sore throat. After a few days, symptoms such as nausea, diarrhoea and vomiting often follow. Many other illnesses, such as malaria, cause similar symptoms which is much more common in returning travellers. Is the NHS prepared? The NHS has well-established processes for managing an Ebola case, including rapid testing and strict infection prevention and control in healthcare settings. The UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) provides clinical advice and testing to the NHS for viral haemorrhagic fevers, including Ebola, and has a test for the strain causing this outbreak in the DRC. What should I do if I think I might have Ebola? Unless you have visited an affected country and been in contact with the body fluids of an infected person, there is very little chance that you have Ebola. If you have visited the DRC or other affected surrounding areas in the last 21 days and you become unwell with symptoms such as fever, chills, muscle aches, vomiting, diarrhoea or a sore throat, you should: stay at home call NHS 111, or 999 in an emergency tell them you have recently travelled to the affected area You should not go to a GP surgery or hospital without calling first. Is there a vaccine or treatment? There are currently no licensed vaccines or therapeutics specific for the Ebola Bundibugyo virus causing the current outbreak. A number of vaccines are currently being developed against the current strain and are being evaluated in clinical trials. ERVEBO is a licensed vaccine approved for the prevention of disease caused by one particular Ebola virus species (Orthoebolavirus zairense). I'm planning to travel to an affected area. What should I do? If you are planning to visit an area affected by the current outbreak, think carefully about your plans and speak to a travel health specialist. You can find advice on the NaTHNaC Ebola disease page and from the FCDO. Organisations sending workers to affected areas, where they may be exposed to Ebola through their work, should register them with the UKHSA Returning Workers Scheme . The scheme has been activated to protect and monitor the health of these workers. UKHSA is closely monitoring the situation and will provide updates if anything changes. A dedicated page on GOV.UK lists outbreaks and case locations of haemorrhagic fevers Ebola and Marburg . Tags: Bundibugyo ebolavirus , ebola , medevac , orthoebolavirus

The incident highlights the UK's commitment to supporting humanitarian workers and managing high-consequence infectious diseases.

news.content_zh: 一名被诊断患有埃博拉病毒的英国援助人员已被医疗撤离至英国接受专科治疗治疗,据英国卫生安全局(UKHSA)报道。该人员通过配备全套个人防护装备(PPE)的医疗撤离航班运送,目前正位于伦敦皇家自由医院的高后果感染性疾病(HCID)单元内。英国已建立完善的系统来管理此类病例,包括快速检测和严格的感染控制协议。对英国公众的风险仍然很低,且在转移过程中埃博拉病毒传播的可能性被认为极低。患者正在隔离治疗,从而最大限度地降低传播传播的风险。英国卫生安全局强调,公众整体风险未发生变化,参与治疗患者的医护人员遵循严格的规程以确保安全。此次事件凸显了英国支持人道主义工作者和管理高后果感染性疾病的承诺。

news.content: Advanced Search Home News Releases Multimedia Meetings Login Register News Release 10-Nov-2026 On the 50th year responding to Ebola: mapping diagnostic, vaccine, and therapeutic gaps across ebolavirus species Peer-Reviewed Publication Higher Education Press Facebook X LinkedIn WeChat Bluesky Message WhatsApp Email image: Evolutionary relationships and pathogenic profiles of Orthoebolaviruses. view more Credit: HIGHER EDUCATION PRESS Fifty years separate the identification of Ebola virus from the outbreak now unfolding, and the interval has produced both remarkable science and a persistent blind spot. The genus Orthoebolavirus contains several species, of which four have caused human illness: Zaire, Sudan, Bundibugyo and Tai Forest. Reston and Bombali viruses have not produced human disease, although serological evidence of exposure exists in people who have contact with infected animals. Zaire virus was identified in 1976 and has driven most recognised outbreaks; Sudan virus appeared in the same year; Bundibugyo virus was first detected in 2007 and has since caused repeated epidemics; Tai Forest virus has produced a single known human case. That distribution of risk explains why one species became the reference strain for countermeasure development and why the others were treated as footnotes. Concentration of effort delivered results. After the 2014-2016 West African epidemic, licensed vaccines, monoclonal antibody cocktails and improved molecular diagnostics moved from experimental platforms into national and international stockpiles, and case fatality fell where they were deployed. The design logic, however, remained single-species. Antigens were drawn from Zaire ebolavirus glycoprotein, antibody cocktails were selected against Zaire epitopes, and diagnostic primers were validated on Zaire genomes. Cross-protection was assumed rather than measured, on the reasoning that glycoprotein is conserved enough for a vaccine to work across the genus. The 2026 Bundibugyo outbreak tested that reasoning in the field. Sequence divergence between species lowers the sensitivity of assays built around Zaire targets, and the result is a double failure: false reassurance when a Zaire-only test is negative in a patient who has filovirus disease, and missed non-Zaire infections that never enter surveillance counts. Vaccines and therapeutics authorized for one species offer uncertain benefit against another, and the uncertainty cannot be resolved in the middle of an emergency. A broader framework is the remedy, and it has concrete components. For diagnostics, conserved pan-ebolavirus targets should be paired with species-specific assays, so that a negative result on a Zaire platform is not read as the absence of disease and so that the responsible species is identified at the point of care rather than weeks later. For vaccines, single-antigen designs should give way to multivalent, mosaic or conserved T-cell epitope platforms, and to constructs that can be updated quickly when antigenic data change. For therapeutics, epitope conservation across species deserves the same scrutiny that affinity for Zaire glycoprotein now receives. All three strands depend on genomic surveillance that is continuous rather than reactive, because mutations affecting primer binding, antigenicity or antibody epitopes must be found before they compromise a stockpile, and because sequence data are what allow a vaccine or assay to be revised on a timescale shorter than an outbreak. Operational readiness forms the last layer, and it is the one most often reduced to inventory. Stockpiles are necessary but not sufficient: unfamiliarity with clinical protocols and pathogen-specific procedures delays response even when guidelines exist on paper. Simulation-based training, including virtual reality modules written for high-consequence infectious disease, can embed procedural competence into routine practice, covering protective equipment donning and doffing, cross-contamination prevention and assessment of suspected special pathogens. Exercises should extend to pathogen identification, rapid diagnostic deployment and the operational machinery that accelerates vaccine and therapeutic development, since none of these capacities can be improvised during an outbreak. The lesson generalises beyond Bundibugyo virus to the wider list of priority pathogens, and it argues for readiness sustained between outbreaks, spanning clinical, public health and laboratory systems, so that the interval between emergence and effective response keeps shortening. None of this is specific to filoviruses, which is the point: the capacity to recognise, isolate and manage an unfamiliar pathogen is generic, and it can be built before the pathogen has a name. analysis_zh.event: 本文报道了应对埃博拉病毒50周年的进展,突出了在埃博拉病毒属各物种中诊断、疫苗和治疗方面的差距。文章指出,2026年的邦迪布古病毒暴发检验了基于扎伊尔病毒的干预措施是否能对其他物种产生交叉保护的假设。
analysis_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 文章指出,扎伊尔病毒是大多数已知暴发的主要原因,而苏丹病毒于1976年首次出现,邦迪布古病毒自2007年以来引发了多次疫情,泰森林病毒仅与单一已知人类病例有关。它还提到,不同物种之间的序列差异降低了检测方法的敏感性,并导致漏检非扎伊尔病毒感染。
analysis_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 文章讨论了应对埃博拉病毒属物种的更广泛框架,包括用于诊断的保守性泛埃博拉病毒靶标、多价疫苗设计以及基于模拟的培训。它还强调了基因组监测和操作准备度的重要性。

analysis.time: The article was published on 2026-11-09. The event date is not explicitly mentioned in the supplied evidence.
analysis.location_and_population: The location is DR Congo, and the affected population includes people exposed to the Bundibugyo virus.
analysis.event: MSF is responding to an Ebola outbreak, specifically mentioning the Bundibugyo virus, and calls for broader access to the ERVEBO vaccine, which was not specifically designed for this virus but may still offer protection.
analysis.scale_impact_and_risk: The scale of impact is not explicitly quantified in the supplied evidence. The risk is not stated, but the article highlights the need for vaccination and medical care.
analysis.response_status_and_uncertainty: MSF is actively responding to the outbreak, and the situation is under investigation. The article does not specify the current status of the outbreak or any official communication.

analysis.brief_en: The article, published on November 9, 2026, by Doctors Without Borders (MSF), discusses their response to an Ebola outbreak in DR Congo. It specifically mentions the Bundibugyo virus and highlights the call for broader access to the ERVEBO vaccine, which, although not designed for this virus, may still provide protection. The article does not provide specific case counts, death counts, or exposure numbers, nor does it mention the current status of the outbreak or any official communication. MSF is actively involved in treating patients and conducting medical research, but the details of the outbreak's scale and risk are not quantified in the supplied evidence. The response is ongoing, and the situation remains under investigation.

news.rss_summary_html: WHO Greenlights Two Ebola Bundibugyo Virus Vaccine Candidates For Phase 2/3 Trials  Health Policy Watch
news.excerpt_original: WHO Greenlights Two Ebola Bundibugyo Virus Vaccine Candidates For Phase 2/3 Trials Health Policy Watch

news.content_title: WHO Greenlights Two Ebola Bundibugyo Virus Vaccine Candidates For Phase 2/3 Trials - Health Policy Watch
news.content: Meg Doherty, Director, Science for Health, announces the WHO recommendation to advance two Bundibugyo Ebolavirus vaccine candidates to Phase2/3 clinical trials. WHO has greenlighted Phase 2/3 trials for two brand new vaccine candidates that specifically target the Ebola Bundibugyo virus species ravaging the Democratic Republic of Congo. Actual trials could forseeably commence “within three to four weeks” – as soon as DRC regulators issue their own approval, said WHO’s Science Director Meg Doherty, at a Wednesday press briefing. The candidates include the ChAdOx1 BDBV , developed by the University of Oxford and the Serum Institute of India, and Moderna’s mRNA-1469 . Doherty said that the preliminary data from animal and Phase human 1 safety trials of the two vaccine candidates had yielded “very positive results” leading to high hopes that the vaccines could indeed protect humans from the Bundibugyo ebolavirus species – for which there is currently no vaccine or treatment. The recommendation was made by the World Health Organization’s Technical Advisory Group on Candidate Vaccines Prioritization (WHO TAG-CVP), and follows their review of the preclinical and Phase 1 clinical data. Initial results expected in early 2027 Ebola Bundibugyo vaccine candidate, ChAdOx1 BDBV, developed by the University of Oxford and the Serum Institute of India, and greenlighted by WHO for Phase 2/3 clinical trials along with Moderna’s mRNA-1469. If all goes well, initial results could then be expected in early 2027. And WHO is meanwhile discussing post-trial access to the vaccine with manufacturers, Doherty said. The two new vaccine candidates will be added to the already ongoing Tumaini Trial , Swahili for ‘hope’, launched on 23 October in Bunia. The same “ring vaccine” trial protocol, which offers immunization to contacts of people who became ill or died from Ebola, will be used for the new candidates, Doherty added. Four vaccination rings are already in place, with several more being prepared. So far, that trial has been testing if the Ervebo vaccine might also offer cross protection against Bundibugyo. Ervebo, developed by MSD, first won European Medicines Agency regulatory approval in 2019 to protect people from the Zaire ebolavirus species, which ravished West Africa in the 2014-2016 Ebola outbreak and then hit again in DRC and other parts of central Africa in 2018-2020. Two vaccine candidate specifically designed to target Bundibugyo DRC Minister of Health Dr Roger Kamba (centre),receives the first consignment of the Ervebo vaccine at N’djili International Airport in Kinshasa on 21 August. The two new vaccine candidates specifically target the Bundibugyo species that’s caused the most recent health emergency, killing over 5,300 people, mostly in DRC, with more than 10,500 cases confirmed . “Do these vaccines show any immunogenicity in animals and non-human primates? And what we are seeing is ‘yes very much so’,” Doherty said. “They’re seeing very positive-looking results that these will be effective in developing immune response.” In terms of human trials , the ChAdOx1 BDBV, a viral vector vaccine. entered its first Phase 1 trial in the United Kingdom on July 24, evaluating safety and immune response in 50 healthy volunteers. In early October, the trial was expanded to Uganda. On 4 August, the mRNA-1469 (Moderna) vaccine candidate commenced a Phase 1 rial in Canada across three sites with roughly 80 volunteers. Research into treatments also advancing Ebola treatment centre in the DRC, epicenter of the outbreak in which more than 10,500 people have been confirmed ill and more than 5,300 have died. The DRC’s Institut National de Recherche Biomédicale , the national public health and biomedical research institute is leading the vaccines trial, with support from the University of Antwerp , Belgium, WHO, Epicentre , Médecins Sans Frontières , the Institute of Tropical Medicine of Antwerp , and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention . The Oslo-based Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI), has been supporting R&D for the two vaccine candidates as well as preliminary research on two additional vaccine candidates under development by the global non-profit biotech research organization, IAVI, in collaboration with Hilleman Laboratories and the UK-based biotech company, Public Health Vaccines . Research into potential treatments is also moving ahead, WHO said in a statement accompanying the TAG recommendations. The WHO-sponsored PARTNERS trial, launched in July, is evaluating whether the monoclonal antibody MBP134, the antiviral remdesivir, or a combination of both can improve survival among patients with confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease. In addition, maftivimab will soon be added to the trial to assess its use as a potential treatment. A complementary post-exposure prophylaxis study with obeldevisir is underway. Said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, “Vaccines alone will not end this outbreak, but they could become a powerful new tool for bringing it under control.” Image Credits: University of Oxford , DRC Health Ministry , WHO Africa . The two new vaccine candidates specifically target the Bundibugyo species that’s caused the most recent health emergency, killing over 5,300 people, mostly in DRC, with more than 10,500 cases confirmed . “Do these vaccines show any immunogenicity in animals and non-human primates? And what we are seeing is ‘yes very much so’,” Doherty said. “They’re seeing very positive-looking results that these will be effective in developing immune response.” In terms of human trials , the ChAdOx1 BDBV, a viral vector vaccine. entered its first Phase 1 trial in the United Kingdom on July 24, evaluating safety and immune response in 50 healthy volunteers. In early October, the trial was expanded to Uganda. On 4 August, the mRNA-1469 (Moderna) vaccine candidate commenced a Phase 1 rial in Canada across three sites with roughly 80 volunteers. Research into treatments also advancing Ebola treatment centre in the DRC, epicenter of the outbreak in which more than 10,500 people have been confirmed ill and more than 5,300 have died. The DRC’s Institut National de Recherche Biomédicale , the national public health and biomedical research institute is leading the vaccines trial, with support from the University of Antwerp , Belgium, WHO, Epicentre , Médecins Sans Frontières , the Institute of Tropical Medicine of Antwerp , and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention . The Oslo-based Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI), has been supporting R&D for the two vaccine candidates as well as preliminary research on two additional vaccine candidates under development by the global non-profit biotech research organization, IAVI, in collaboration with Hilleman Laboratories and the UK-based biotech company, Public Health Vaccines . Research into potential treatments is also moving ahead, WHO said in a statement accompanying the TAG recommendations. The WHO-sponsored PARTNERS trial, launched in July, is evaluating whether the monoclonal antibody MBP134, the antiviral remdesivir, or a combination of both can improve survival among patients with confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease. In addition, maftivimab will soon be added to the trial to assess its use as a potential treatment. A complementary post-exposure prophylaxis study with obeldevisir is underway. Said Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, “Vaccines alone will not end this outbreak, but they could become a powerful new tool for bringing it under control.” Image Credits: University of Oxford , DRC Health Ministry , WHO Africa . news.excerpt: NCDC says Nigeria has recorded no additional Ebola case, 21 days after confirming an imported infection of the Bundibugyo virus from Uganda.
news.rss_summary_html: NCDC says Nigeria has recorded no additional Ebola case, 21 days after confirming an imported infection of the Bundibugyo virus from Uganda.

news.content_title: 28 contacts still under surveillance -NCDC gives update on Ebola in Nigeria
news.content: BREAKING: Flamingos conquer Japan to win historic first U-17 Women’s World Cup title Follow Us: Today’s Paper (opens in a new tab) Nigerian News Top Stories Entertainment Politics Sports Business Fact Check Read Today’s Paper (opens in a new tab) LIVE SCORES: Football › Health 28 contacts still under surveillance -NCDC gives update on Ebola in Nigeria Published By Ayorinde Oluokun Date 11th November, 2026 Share: Dr. Jide Idris, NCDC boss Quick Read NCDC explained that being identified as a contact did not mean an individual had Ebola, stressing that monitoring enabled early detection and prompt response to symptoms. By Franca Ofili The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) said Nigeria has recorded no additional Ebola case, 21 days after confirming an imported infection of the Bundibugyo virus from Uganda. It however said 28 contacts still remained under active surveillance for Ebola disease in the country. The Director-General of the NCDC, Dr Jide Idris, disclosed this in a national health security update issued on Tuesday. Idris said the agency had identified 62 contacts, with 34 completing their individual 21-day monitoring period, while 28 remained under surveillance. He explained that being identified as a contact did not mean an individual had Ebola, stressing that monitoring enabled early detection and prompt response to symptoms. “NCDC is sustaining contact tracing, laboratory testing, surveillance, infection prevention and investigation of reported alerts in collaboration with relevant federal and state authorities,” Idris said. He urged healthcare workers in public and private facilities to remain vigilant, establish patients’ travel and exposure histories, and immediately report suspected Ebola cases to public health authorities. Idris advised anyone developing symptoms after possible exposure to avoid contact with others and call the NCDC toll-free line, 6232, for guidance before visiting a health facility. He said dengue fever had been confirmed in Sokoto and Zamfara States, while Chikungunya was confirmed in Sokoto, prompting intensified surveillance and response activities. The NCDC boss said National Rapid Response Teams, including entomologists from the National Arbovirus Research Centre, Enugu, had been deployed to support affected states. He said the teams were assisting with case identification, laboratory investigations, clinical readiness, community engagement and mosquito control to contain the infections. Idris warned Nigerians against assuming that every fever was malaria, noting that dengue and Chikungunya could cause fever, headaches, body pains and joint pains. He urged people experiencing persistent fever, rash, vomiting or severe joint pains to seek medical assessment, warning that dengue could become life-threatening when warning signs were ignored. He advised households to eliminate stagnant water, cover water containers, clear discarded tyres and protect themselves against mosquito bites, noting that disease-carrying mosquitoes often bite during the daytime. On cerebrospinal meningitis, Idris said the agency was strengthening preparedness as the dry season advanced, with increased risks in parts of the meningitis belt. He urged states to improve disease surveillance, diagnostic services, clinical readiness and vaccination responses, where indicated, to prevent avoidable deaths. He urged Nigerians experiencing sudden fever, severe headache, neck stiffness or confusion to seek urgent medical attention, while advising health facilities to promptly identify and refer suspected cases. The NCDC director-general said diphtheria remained a concern, particularly among children who had missed routine immunisation, adding that the agency was supporting surveillance, laboratory diagnosis and outbreak response. He urged parents and caregivers to check their children’s vaccination status and seek guidance on missed doses, stressing that vaccination and early treatment were essential. By Franca Ofili The Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) said Nigeria has recorded no additional Ebola case, 21 days after confirming an imported infection of the Bundibugyo virus from Uganda. It however said 28 contacts still remained under active surveillance for Ebola disease in the country. The Director-General of the NCDC, Dr Jide Idris, disclosed this in a national health security update issued on Tuesday. Idris said the agency had identified 62 contacts, with 34 completing their individual 21-day monitoring period, while 28 remained under surveillance. He explained that being identified as a contact did not mean an individual had Ebola, stressing that monitoring enabled early detection and prompt response to symptoms. “NCDC is sustaining contact tracing, laboratory testing, surveillance, infection prevention and investigation of reported alerts in collaboration with relevant federal and state authorities,” Idris said. He urged healthcare workers in public and private facilities to remain vigilant, establish patients’ travel and exposure histories, and immediately report suspected Ebola cases to public health authorities. Idris advised anyone developing symptoms after possible exposure to avoid contact with others and call the NCDC toll-free line, 6232, for guidance before visiting a health facility. He said dengue fever had been confirmed in Sokoto and Zamfara States, while Chikungunya was confirmed in Sokoto, prompting intensified surveillance and response activities. The NCDC boss said National Rapid Response Teams, including entomologists from the National Arbovirus Research Centre, Enugu, had been deployed to support affected states. He said the teams were assisting with case identification, laboratory investigations, clinical readiness, community engagement and mosquito control to contain the infections. Idris warned Nigerians against assuming that every fever was malaria, noting that dengue and Chikungunya could cause fever, headaches, body pains and joint pains. He urged people experiencing persistent fever, rash, vomiting or severe joint pains to seek medical assessment, warning that dengue could become life-threatening when warning signs were ignored. He advised households to eliminate stagnant water, cover water containers, clear discarded tyres and protect themselves against mosquito bites, noting that disease-carrying mosquitoes often bite during the daytime. On cerebrospinal meningitis, Idris said the agency was strengthening preparedness as the dry season advanced, with increased risks in parts of the meningitis belt. He urged states to improve disease surveillance, diagnostic services, clinical readiness and vaccination responses, where indicated, to prevent avoidable deaths. He urged Nigerians experiencing sudden fever, severe headache, neck stiffness or confusion to seek urgent medical attention, while advising health facilities to promptly identify and refer suspected cases. The NCDC director-general said diphtheria remained a concern, particularly among children who had missed routine immunisation, adding that the agency was supporting surveillance, laboratory diagnosis and outbreak response. He urged parents and caregivers to check their children’s vaccination status and seek guidance on missed doses, stressing that vaccination and early treatment were essential. Idris said fever accompanied by sore throat, neck swelling, difficulty swallowing or breathing required prompt medical assessment to prevent complications from diphtheria. On Lassa fever, he said Nigeria was approaching the period when cases historically increased, urging states to strengthen surveillance, testing, treatment readiness and infection prevention before the seasonal peak. He called on health facilities to ensure adequate supplies, trained personnel and safe referral arrangements, while protecting frontline workers against infection. He advised households to protect food from rodents, store food in covered containers and maintain clean surroundings, urging people with persistent fever to seek early medical attention. Idris also urged clinicians to consider other possible infections beyond malaria when assessing patients with persistent fever, particularly during the Lassa fever season. Ahead of the festive period, he called on state governments, event organisers and healthcare providers to strengthen health and safety arrangements for concerts, religious gatherings and other mass events. He urged event organisers to provide basic medical assistance, maintain hygiene and sanitation, and establish clear procedures for identifying and reporting suspected infectious diseases. He also advised travellers and participants at gatherings to follow public health advisories, seek medical attention when unwell and avoid crowded events when experiencing symptoms. “State governments have to sustain surveillance, laboratory capacity, treatment readiness and community engagement, while providing frontline workers with adequate funding and operational resources,” Idris advised. He urged public and private health facilities to promptly report suspected infections and implement appropriate measures to protect healthcare personnel. Idris advised Nigerians to ensure children were fully vaccinated, protect themselves against mosquitoes and rodents, seek medical attention early and avoid spreading unverified information. He said Nigerians could report suspected cases or obtain guidance through the NCDC toll-free line, 6232, or their respective state public health authorities. The NCDC boss said the Ebola response remained active, alongside interventions against dengue, Chikungunya and diphtheria, as the country strengthened preparedness for meningitis and Lassa fever. news.content_zh: 尼日利亚疾病控制与预防中心(NCDC)更新了尼日利亚埃博拉疫情的最新情况,指出仍有28名接触者处于主动监测状态。这源于从乌干达确认了一例输入性邦迪布古病毒感染,且在21天后未报告新增病例。NCDC强调,被认定为接触者并不等同于感染埃博拉病毒,监测有助于早期发现和应对。主任贾迪·艾德里斯博士指出,正在进行接触者追踪、实验室检测和监测工作,呼吁医护人员保持警惕并及时报告疑似病例。此外,NCDC还提及其他健康问题,如登革热、基孔肯雅热、白喉和拉沙热,强调公众意识和准备的重要性。该机构还建议家庭消除积水、盖好食物容器,并防范蚊虫和鼠类叮咬。总体而言,应对工作仍在持续,团队已部署至受影响州以支持并防止不必要的死亡。

supplementary_news.content: You need to enable JavaScript to run this app. Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites Latest videos Latest audio Regions Africa Asia Europe Latin America Middle East North America Germany Topics Climate Equality Health Human Rights Migration Technology Categories Business Science Environment Culture Sports In focus COP31Ukraine warNvidia Latest audioLatest videos Live TV Advertisement HealthAfrica Ebola: Why is there still no vaccine? Hannah Fuchs 11/07/2026November 7, 2026 Ebola has been known about for decades, but there is still no vaccine against the Bundibugyo strain of the virus causing the current outbreak. New research raises hopes of protection against the various types of Ebola. https://p.dw.com/p/5PCYI Copy link Prefer DW on Google Researchers are working to develop a vaccine against the strain of Ebola responsible for the current outbreak Image: Sebastien Kitsa Musayi/AP Photo/picture alliance Advertisement 1976: A hitherto unknown disease breaks out near the Ebola river in the country then known as Zaire, now the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). This was the first scientifically documented Ebola epidemic. Now, 50 years on, the DRC once again finds itself at the center of a major Ebola outbreak. This time the pathogen is the less common Bundibugyo type of the genus orthoebolavirus. The virus was identified in 2007 during an outbreak in Bundibugyo, Uganda. Another outbreak occurred in the DRC in 2012. Preparations could have been made for Bundibugyo How can a virus that has been known for decades continue to infect thousands of people, yet there is still no licensed vaccine or official treatment? Torsten Feldt, a doctor of tropical medicine at Düsseldorf's University Hospital, sees this as a missed opportunity. "We had come across the Bundibugyo virus in two previous outbreaks: 2007 in Uganda and 2012 in DR Congo. So we had enough time to develop vaccines and therapeutic options. But we didn't make use of this opportunity, meaning crucial time was lost during the current outbreak," he said. Leonie Mayer from the German Center for Infection Research (DZIF) and the Institute for Infection Research and Vaccine Development at the University Medical Center in Hamburg-Eppendorf agrees. "They could of course have developed a vaccine and run pre-clinical trials before," Mayer told DW. She stressed, however, that their effectiveness can only be assessed and confirmed during an actual outbreak. Mayer is the lead author of a recently published study that examined whether Ervebo, an Ebola vaccine that has already been licensed, can be used against other types of Ebola as well. Congo's Ebola crisis: Fear, mistrust and a growing outbreak To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video 12:34 Why Ebola is a good candidate for vaccine development From an immunological point of view, and compared to — for example — influenza or HIV, Ebola is a very worthwhile candidate for a vaccine. Influenza viruses are constantly mutating, and the human immunodeficiency virus is particularly good at evading our immune defenses. Ebola is far more predictable. "I think — and perhaps it's kind of a blessing in disguise — that it will be relatively straightforward to develop a vaccine against Bundibugyo," said Mayer. Herein lies the paradox. From a scientific point of view, Ebola is a good vaccine candidate, yet there is still no licensed form of prevention against the Bundibugyo variant that is currently circulating. Mayer explained that vaccines cannot be developed as a precautionary measure against every potential pathogen. Lack of funding or the prioritization of other pathogens often have a role to play. Many researchers had assumed that a fresh outbreak of the Sudan Ebola virus was more likely, and vaccine development for this strain is more advanced. Different types of Ebola Another part of the problem is that Ebola is not one single virus. The known, highly dangerous orthoebolaviruses include Ebola virus (EBOV), previously called the Zaire Ebola virus (ZEBOV), the Sudan virus (SUDV), and the Bundibugyo virus (BDBV). The existing vaccine, Ervebo, was developed and licensed for use against the Zaire variant. But there is still no approved protection against the others. This is why the existing Ebola vaccine has been of only limited use to people in the areas of the current outbreak. Another factor may also be relevant: The Bundibugyo virus appears to be less aggressive than the Zaire variant. At first, that sounds like good news, but it may make it harder to contain, as people remain mobile for longer after being infected, and can pass on the virus without realizing. Ervebo vaccine shows immune response to Bundibugyo In the recently published study, Mayer's research team from the DZIF investigated whether the already licensed Ebola vaccine could trigger an immune response not only against EBOV, but against other types of Ebola as well. They found cross-reactive T-cell responses against Bundibugyo, and also, to a lesser extent, against the Sudan virus. For Mayer, this is already an important finding. "We now know that the immune cells can most likely also recognize the Bundibugyo virus," she said. "Our data does not enable us to answer the question of whether this immune response actually provides protection, or if it results in a milder progression of the disease," she added, calling it an important gap in our knowledge. Advertisement Why can't existing vaccine be deployed yet? If there's a vaccine that has already been licensed, and indications that it could protect people, why isn't it simply being deployed? Mayer explains the dilemma. For one thing, she said, it's not ethical to deploy a vaccine if you're not sure whether or how well it works. Also, if it were used on a large scale, it would no longer be possible to establish whether it actually works: A reduction in cases could also be a result of other measures, or the epidemic might already have passed its peak. Jürgen May, a specialist in tropical diseases at the Bernhard Nocht Institute, also warns against mass vaccination. "Mass vaccination without proof of efficacy could create a false sense of security, forfeit trust, and, if it does not provide sufficient protection, make study impossible," he said. It's very important for there to be acceptance on the ground. "If we inoculate people with a vaccine on a large scale, and afterwards it turns out that it was nothing like as effective as we expected, it's very difficult to communicate that to people on the ground," Mayer said. In a worst-case scenario, people could subsequently refuse inoculation with more effective vaccines. Why Ebola is still so difficult to contain But the current outbreak also shows that medical innovation alone is not enough. Conflicts, difficult transport routes, attacks on healthcare facilities and gaps in contact tracing all make it harder to contain. Congo has had more than 10,000 cases of Bundibugyo since May. Recently, it has also been reported in Kenya and NigeriaImage: Andrew Kasuku/AP Photo/dpa/picture alliance Torsten Feldt said identifying Bundibugyo is no longer a problem in itself. What is often limiting is the practical availability of diagnostic tools. "In remote or conflict-affected regions, samples often have to be transported over long distances," he explained. Here we see another Ebola paradox. The world is getting ever better at diagnosing infections, but it still struggles to contain outbreaks fast enough. The authors of an article in the current issue of Nature come to the same conclusion: The problem is often not identifying cases, but the speed with which people react. Finding Ebola is often easier now than stopping Ebola, they wrote. From a Bundibugyo vaccine to a pan-Ebola one? Many researchers believe the current crisis could potentially also provide a great opportunity. The so-called Tumaini study, which is testing different vaccine candidates, has now been launched in Congo. These include Ervebo, developed by Oxford University, and a Moderna mRNA vaccine. The study aims to provide the first reliable data about their efficacy against the Bundibugyo virus. Whether these vaccines could still help control the current outbreak is uncertain. There is hope, but experts estimate that, realistically, it will be several months before any such vaccine is available for widespread use; perhaps not until mid-2027. "Ideally, we will develop cross-reactive pan-Ebola vaccines," Christof Geldmacher, a co-author of the DZIF study, said of their long-term plans. This is also something that is being worked on. For now, though, the focus is on developing an effective vaccine against the Bundibugyo variant of the virus. This article was originally written in German. supplementary_news.content_title: 病例破万:刚果(金)埃博拉疫情暴发,已跨境蔓延多国_腾讯新闻
supplementary_news.content: 病例破万:刚果(金)埃博拉疫情暴发,已跨境蔓延多国 QuriositySISU 2026-11-07 18:07发布于上海国际领域创作者 问AI · 民众不信任防疫的深层历史原因有哪些? 阅读时长|6min Since mid‐May, the Bundibugyo‐strain Ebola outbreak has caused 5,026 deaths out of 10,351 confirmed cases in the DRC. It has spread to Uganda, Kenya and Nigeria, with repeated attacks on health workers disrupting epidemic response. 今年5月中旬宣布暴发以来,刚果(金)由本迪布焦型病毒引发的埃博拉疫情累计确诊 10351 例,死亡 5026 例。疫情已外溢至乌干达、肯尼亚、尼日利亚等邻国。受东部武装冲突、民众不信任等因素影响,国内抗疫形势严峻,针对防疫人员的暴力事件频发,防控工作阻力重重。 本轮疫情从刚果(金)的伊图里省逐步扩散至全国8个省份。成为该国历史上死亡人数最多、扩散最快的埃博拉疫情,如今疫情进入高位平台期,每周仍新增约 400 至 500 例,由于疫苗尚处于试验阶段,当前仅能对症救治,疫情仍未得到有效控制,其严重程度仅次于2014年至2016年间西非的疫情。专家担忧,若疫情形势持续恶化,可能演变为史上最严重的埃博拉疫情。 此外,人员跨境流动已造成病毒外溢:乌干达最先出现境外输入病例;肯尼亚累计9例确诊、2例死亡;尼日利亚发现1例输入病例。10月28日,非洲疾控中心召开非洲卫生部长线上峰会,呼吁联防联控,密切监测跨境人员流动。 2026年9月26日,刚果东部贝尼市埃博拉治疗中心,一名身穿防护服的医护人员正在接受消毒 | 图源:美联社 本轮疫情病原体为本迪布焦型埃博拉病毒(Bundibugyo-strain Ebola virus, BDBV),属埃博拉病毒中较罕见的亚型,相较于扎伊尔型等高致死率常见毒株,本迪布焦型传播认知更少、临床救治经验匮乏,全球暂无商业化疫苗与特效药,仅可采取基础对症治疗与隔离阻断传播。此前仅在乌干达有过两次报告疫情,非洲多国基层疾控系统对其识别、处置能力普遍薄弱。 埃博拉病毒1976年首次在刚果和苏丹南部被识别,主要通过接触感染者的体液传播,果蝠被认为其天然宿主。 专家推测,刚果(金)伊图里省的疫情早于官方宣布数月就已开始传播,且此前的检测多针对更常见的病毒类型,延误了病毒的早期识别。 本轮埃博拉跨境暴发已形成区域性公共卫生危机,对非洲东、中、西部多国造成连锁冲击。多国被迫收紧出入境防疫政策、暂停部分跨境商贸与民间往来,局部地区人道主义物资运输受阻。 世卫组织与美国疾控中心(CDC)模型共同预警:当前病毒隐匿传播链条未被切断,若社区抵制、战乱干扰问题持续得不到解决,本次疫情极有可能刷新本世纪埃博拉疫情最高感染纪录,对全球传染病防控体系构成严峻挑战。 然而,受东部武装冲突、民众不信任、政府应对乏力等多重因素影响,该国国内针对防疫人员的暴力事件频发、民众反对声浪迭起、防控工作阻力重重。 5月疫情初期,伊图里省首府布尼亚的红十字会志愿者遭居民扔石头攻击、言语辱骂;多处医疗帐篷被纵火破坏;部分防控小队成员被居民扣留;安全殡葬小队也屡遭威胁。 9月末,曾公开倡导防疫举措的地方官员玛丽-塞莱斯坦・卡伦德瓦(Marie-Célestin Karondwa)在北基伍省的家中遭反对防控的愤怒居民殴打致死,其房屋也被纵火焚烧。 10月24日,刚果(金)的特肖波省,一名护士出诊排查疑似病例时遇害,另有一名同行医护工作者受重伤。 2026年5月25日,刚果(金)布尼亚,红十字会志愿者瓦妮・比龙吉(Vanny Birungi)在埃博拉疫情期间向民众开展防疫宣传。 | 图源:美联社 联合国曾将刚果(金)东部冲突称为 “地球上最旷日持久、最复杂、最严重的人道主义危机之一”。这场危机始于1994年卢旺达大屠杀,大量武装难民涌入刚果(金)东部,引爆了两次大规模刚果战争。战后,中央政府难以管控东部,数十支武装团体长期割据、争夺资源,冲突数十年难以平息。 疫情暴发地正是刚果(金)东部战乱最严重的地区。卢旺达支持的“M23”反政府武装等多个武装团体在此长期争夺立足点。东部战乱导致人道主义救援通行受阻,疾控人员难以深入疫区完成密接追踪。 民众的不信任和谣言是疫情防控的另一大障碍,许多人否认病毒存在,将其视为 “白人发明的骗局”,拒绝报告病例、隔离治疗与安全殡葬;政府腐败、此前疫情处置不力积累的不信任,让居民对外来防疫队伍充满警惕。 约70%新增病例无法追溯至已登记的密切接触者,病毒脱离追踪,正处于隐匿传播状态。至少60%的死亡发生于医院外,大量感染病例未被统计。 "These are people we never had opportunity to try to save them and it is one of the biggest concerns for us in this outbreak. How do we try to reach people early to get them to come to health facilities to get a fighting chance to survive?" “我们甚至尚未有机会尝试拯救他们,这是我们这次疫情中最大的担忧之一——我们如何尽早接触到感染病毒的人们,让他们来到医疗机构,争取存活的机会?”世界卫生组织项目区域经理帕特里克·奥蒂姆(Patrick Otim)医生说。 同时,抗疫前线人力危机持续。伊图里、北基伍的医护人员多次威胁罢工,以抗议当地政府数月欠薪、防护物资短缺,部分医疗中心服务一度停滞。 埃博拉疫情的蔓延也为居民带来巨大心理创伤。在疫情中痛失亲人本就令人难以承受。然而在当地,由于谣言与认知误区,不少民众将埃博拉病毒引发的症状视作邪祟,这种对病人的偏见与歧视使悲痛变得更加沉重。同时,病毒传播风险限制了家属与逝者的接触,人们无法按本民族习俗举办葬礼,难以完成与家人的告别。 "Grief, fear of infection, social isolation and a succession of deaths can leave families and communities lastingly vulnerable." 当地精神卫生机构的护士长阿尼塞特·卡滕博·维亚卢瓦(Anicet Katembo Vyaluva)表示:“悲伤、对感染的恐惧、社会隔离以及接连不断的死亡,会让家庭和社区长期处于脆弱状态。” 10月15日,刚果(金)布尼亚,一位女性在心理治疗中心接受心理健康援助。她的两位亲人不幸死于埃博拉。 | 图源:美联社 目前,当局正推行以村庄为中心的社区防控,依靠村庄领袖开展密接追踪、安全殡葬与病例隔离。 世卫组织将本次疫情列为国际关注的突发公共卫生事件,联动非洲疾控中心推动跨境防疫协作,号召无国界医生投入一线救治;并组织疫苗试验同步开展,针对本迪布焦病毒的候选疫苗临床试验已在伊图里省启动,专家希望明年能有一款有效疫苗可用。 但世卫组织官员警告疫情 “远未受控”,根据美国疾控预防中心的模型预测,未来三个月,病例数可能飙升至2万以上。 编译|李家济 排版|何倩

supplementary_news.content_title: WHO adds two Bundibugyo vaccines to Ebola trial in the DRC
supplementary_news.content: Two experimental vaccines made to fight a type of Ebola virus that is behind the outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) will be added to the country's Tumaini clinical trial, the World Health Organization (WHO) said in a recent news release. The vaccines—ChAdOx1 BDBV, which comes from the University of Oxford and the Serum Institute of India, and Moderna's mRNA-1469—were added to combat Bundibugyo. A WHO advisory group recommended both vaccines for more testing this week, based on lab, animal and early human data. They will join the trial once national approvals are in place. WHO said this is the first time vaccines built for the Bundibugyo virus will be tested during an outbreak. “Vaccines alone will not end this outbreak, but they could become a powerful new tool for bringing it under control,” Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Ph.D., WHO director-general, said in the release. What is Bundibugyo virus disease? Three viruses are known to cause large Ebola outbreaks: Ebola virus (often called the Zaire type), Sudan virus and Bundibugyo virus, according to the WHO Ebola fact sheet. Fruit bats are thought to carry the viruses in nature. People catch it through direct contact with an infected person's blood or body fluids, or with surfaces those fluids have touched. People can't spread it before they have symptoms. Symptoms show up 2 to 21 days after infection and often start suddenly. Early signs include fever, fatigue, muscle pain and headache. After, patients may have vomiting, diarrhea, rash and kidney and liver problems. On average, about half of people with Ebola die, WHO says, though past outbreaks have ranged from 25% to 90%. Bundibugyo virus was first found in 2007 in the Bundibugyo district of western Uganda. A second outbreak hit the DRC in 2012, according to the UK Health Security Agency. The current outbreak began in May. It is now the largest Bundibugyo outbreak on record and the second-largest Ebola outbreak ever. As of late October, the DRC had reported 10,193 confirmed cases and 4,960 deaths across eight provinces, according to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC). Cases tied to the outbreak have also turned up in Kenya and Nigeria. According to the release, there is a major gap in tools to fight it. The approved Ebola vaccines—Ervebo (Ebola Zaire vaccine) and the two-dose Zabdeno (Ad26.ZEBOV) and Mvabea (MVA-BN-Filo) regimen—work only against the Zaire type. The same is true of the two approved antibody treatments, Ebanga (ansuvimab-zykl) and Inmazeb (atoltivimab, maftivimab and odesivimab-ebgn). How the Tumaini Ebola vaccine trial works Meaning "hope" in Swahili, the Tumaini phase 2/3 trial gave its first shot in late October in Bunia, the capital of Ituri province and the center of the outbreak, the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI) said in a news release. Ervebo was the first vaccine tested to see whether it also protects against Bundibugyo. The trial can test several vaccines under one plan. It uses ring vaccination, which means vaccinating the contacts of people with confirmed cases. A similar trial in Guinea about a decade ago proved Ervebo worked against the Zaire type. Four vaccination rings are in place, and more are being set up. The DRC's Institut National de Recherche Biomédicale and Belgium's University of Antwerp lead the trial. WHO, Médecins Sans Frontières and other groups are partners, and CEPI is funding vaccine development. “There is still no licensed vaccine against Bundibugyo virus, and the cost of that absence is being counted in the DRC every day, in lives lost and in health workers who go to work without protection” Richard Hatchett, M.D., CEO of CEPI, said when the trial launched. Treatment research for Bundibugyo virus disease Researchers are also testing treatments. The WHO-sponsored PARTNERS trial, which began in July, is studying whether patients are more likely to survive if they get the experimental antibody MBP134, the antiviral Veklury (remdesivir) or both. Maftivimab, one of the three antibodies in Inmazeb, will soon be added to the trial. A separate study, EBO-PEP, is testing whether an experimental antiviral pill, obeldesivir, can keep high-risk contacts from getting sick. Early results from the treatment trial are expected in the coming months, and vaccine results are expected in early 2027, WHO said. Tedros called the vaccines' readiness for testing “a testament to the power of science and partnership.”

Facebook Twitter Print Email Two new Ebola vaccines to join DR Congo clinical trial 5 November 2026 Health Two new Ebola vaccine candidates will be added to a clinical trial in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) as the country continues to battle a deadly outbreak caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus. The announcement by the UN World Health Organization (WHO) follows the recommendation of its independent Technical Advisory Group on Candidate Vaccines Prioritization. This will mark the first time that vaccines specifically designed for Bundibugyo virus will be evaluated during an outbreak of the disease. “The fact that these vaccines are ready to enter clinical trials is a testament to the power of science and partnership,” said WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus. Tweet URL He stressed that while vaccines alone will not end the outbreak, “they could become a powerful new tool for bringing it under control”. ‘Hope’ as cases mount The two vaccine candidates are ChAdOx1, developed by the University of Oxford with the Serum Institute of India, and mRNA-1469, developed by the American pharmaceutical and biotech company Moderna. WHO convened the expert group which this week recommended them for further clinical evaluation, based on available evidence. The DRC has been battling a deadly outbreak of Ebola disease caused by the rare Bundibugyo virus species for nearly six months and it has become the largest in the country’s history. As of 1 November, there were more than 10,500 confirmed cases and 5,126 deaths. WHO is supporting the Tumaini multi-vaccine trial, named after the Swahili word for “hope”. It was launched on 23 October in the eastern city of Bunia, capital of Ituri province, which remains the epicentre of the outbreak. The Ervebo vaccine, used to treat the Zaire species of the Ebola virus, is already being tested to determine if it is effective against Bundibugyo species. The two new vaccine candidates will enter the trial following national approvals. Tumaini is designed to test multiple vaccine candidates within a single trial, using a ring-vaccination approach that focuses on contacts of people with confirmed Ebola Bundibugyo. WHO and partners pioneered the strategy during the West Africa Ebola outbreak a decade ago, where a trial in Guinea established the efficacy of the Ervebo vaccine. Four vaccination rings have been set up and several more are being prepared, while research into other potential treatments is also moving forward. Britannica Editors Last updated Nov. 5, 2026 •History Britannica AI Ask Anything Table of Contents Table of Contents Ask Anything Viewed through an electron microscope, ebolaviruses appear as long filaments, sometimes branched or intertwined. The virion (virus particle) contains one molecule of noninfectious single-stranded RNA (ribonucleic acid). It is not known how the viruses attack cells; it has been postulated that they produce proteins that suppress the immune system, allowing reproduction of virus to continue unhindered. Viral hemorrhagic fevers similar to Ebola typically are carried by arthropods and rodents, but the natural reservoirs for ebolaviruses are yet to be discovered. Among the suspected reservoirs for Ebola are bats, primates, rodents, and insects that inhabit tropical forests in Africa and Asia. Ebola can be transmitted through contact with infected blood and bodily fluids as well as through contact with surfaces or objects contaminated by those fluids. The virus has also been detected in the organs of patients after recovery from the fever. In men, the virus may remain infectious in semen for as long as two months following return to health. Unsanitary conditions and lack of adequate medical supplies may be factors in the spread of the disease. Burial rituals that involve close contact with the body of a person who has died from the disease also can result in the spread of Ebola. The surfaces of bodies of deceased victims remain infectious for more than a week. In addition, a small percentage of Ebola-infected individuals may remain asymptomatic; such persons may unknowingly carry and spread the virus. Ebolaviruses have an incubation period of 2 to 21 days. The onset of illness is sudden and harsh. Infected persons may develop fever, severe headaches and muscle aches, and loss of appetite. Within a few days the virus causes a condition known as disseminated intravascular coagulation, which is marked by both blood clots and hemorrhaging. In the case of Ebola, clots are concentrated in the liver, spleen, brain, and other internal organs, forcing capillaries to bleed into surrounding tissue. Nausea, vomiting and diarrhea with blood and mucus, conjunctivitis, and sore throat soon follow. A maculopapular rash (discolored elevations of the skin) appears on the trunk and quickly spreads to the limbs and head. The patient is then beset by spontaneous bleeding from body orifices and any breaks in the skin, such as injection sites, and within the gastrointestinal tract, skin, and internal organs. Death is usually brought on by hemorrhaging, shock, or renal failure and occurs within 8 to 17 days. Persons who survive Ebola infection may experience post-Ebola syndrome, symptoms of which include vision problems (potentially blindness), headaches, severe joint and muscle pain, and extreme fatigue. Treatment Treatment for Ebola is primarily with supportive care, including fluids, electrolytes, and medications to stabilize blood pressure and manage complications. Early treatment greatly improves survival. For infections caused by the Zaire strain of Ebola virus, targeted antibody therapies such as REGN-EB3 (Inmazeb) and mAb114 (Ebanga) can help reduce mortality. Other treatments that had been investigated for Ebola included the antiviral drug remdesivir (RDV) and ZMapp, a mixture of three antibodies that bind to proteins on ebolaviruses. ZMapp was administered to infected individuals during the 2014–16 outbreak, though its effectiveness was unclear. In trials during the 2018–20 Ebola outbreak, both REGN-EB3 and mAb114 were found to be more effective at reducing Ebola-related mortality compared with RDV and ZMapp. REGN-EB3 and mAb114 were approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) in 2020. Ebola virus disease; hand washingA Liberian nurse washing his hands with water after treating a patient sick with Ebola virus disease in Monrovia, Liberia, during the 2014–15 outbreak.(more) The spread of ebolaviruses can be contained by barrier nursing, handling of infected blood and tissue in isolated laboratory units, and proper decontamination of reusable equipment. Experimental vaccines are under development for Ebola, including a vaccine known as VSV-EBOV, which was found to be highly effective in preventing the spread of ebolavirus among persons in close contact with infected individuals. VSV-EBOV was a recombinant vesicular stomatitis virus (VSV)-based vaccine that expressed an EBOV glycoprotein. When VSV-EBOV was injected, the vaccinated individuals generated antibodies against the EBOV protein, thereby gaining immunity. Survivors of Ebola infection may be affected by a constellation of long-term health complications known as post-Ebola syndrome. In follow-up studies of persons who recovered from acute Ebola infection, many were found to suffer from uveitis (eye redness and pain), vision loss, tinnitus, hearing loss, stroke, headaches, muscle and joint pain, and other abnormalities in musculoskeletal and neurological function. Some affected individuals also suffered renal failure and were at increased risk of premature death. Post-Ebola syndrome is treated primarily by symptom management with drugs such as analgesics (pain relievers) and anti-inflammatory agents. Britannica Editors History Britannica AI Ask Anything Table of Contents Table of Contents Ask Anything Top Questions What are viral hemorrhagic fevers? Viral hemorrhagic fevers are a group of highly dangerous illnesses caused by viruses that damage the vascular system, leading to severe bleeding. Initial symptoms include fever, fatigue, muscle aches, and exhaustion. These viruses belong to four families: Flaviviridae, Arenaviridae, Bunyaviridae, and Filoviridae. Specific animals or insects often transmit them, restricting these diseases to certain geographic areas. Examples include dengue, yellow fever, Lassa fever, and Ebola. Transmission to humans usually occurs via contact with infected animals like rodents and insects. Avoiding contact with these hosts and controlling their populations can prevent infection. Isolation of infected individuals can also prevent the virus from spreading from person to person. 2 Britannica Sources viral hemorrhagic fever bloodborne disease: Common bloodborne diseases Created from Britannica articles using AI. AI can make mistakes, so verify using Britannica articles. Which viruses can cause viral hemorrhagic fevers? Viral hemorrhagic fevers (VHFs) are a group of severe illnesses characterized by bleeding, fever, and shock. These diseases are caused by viruses from four families: Flaviviridae, Arenaviridae, Bunyaviridae, and Filoviridae. Flaviviruses Dengue and yellow fever viruses, often transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes, are the most common causes. While yellow fever affects the liver and causes severe bleeding, dengue induces only minor bleeding but can result in dengue shock syndrome. Arenaviruses are spread to humans through contact with food or soil contaminated by rodent excreta. This family of viruses causes Lassa fever, Argentine hemorrhagic fever, Bolivian hemorrhagic fever, Brazilian hemorrhagic fever, and Venezuelan hemorrhagic fever. Bunyaviridae includes Hantaviruses, Rift Valley fever virus, and Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus. Hantaviruses are transmitted to humans through rodent contact, while Rift Valley fever is a mosquito-borne disease. Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever is a tick-borne disease. Filoviruses such as Ebola virus and Marburg virus, are highly fatal and may also cause disease in primates. The origin of filovirus epidemics remains unclear, but scientists suspect that fruit bats may be responsible for outbreaks of Marburg disease. 2 Britannica Sources viral hemorrhagic fever bloodborne disease: Common bloodborne diseases Created from Britannica articles using AI. AI can make mistakes, so verify using Britannica articles. How do viral hemorrhagic fevers affect the human body? Viral hemorrhagic fevers (VHFs) are a group of highly dangerous illnesses caused by bloodborne viruses that harm the vascular system, resulting in significant bleeding. Initial symptoms include fever, fatigue, and muscle aches. The viruses attack cells and may suppress the immune system, which allows the virus to reproduce. Disseminated intravascular coagulation, a condition marked by blood clots and hemorrhaging, can occur. Clots concentrated in organs force capillaries to bleed into surrounding tissue. This leads to bleeding from body openings, the gastrointestinal tract, skin, and internal organs. Some VHFs, such as dengue, induce only minor bleeding that is rarely fatal, while others, such as Ebola, can cause death in up to 90% of victims. 4 Britannica Sources viral hemorrhagic fever Ebola: Course of infection Marburgvirus bloodborne disease: Common bloodborne diseases Created from Britannica articles using AI. AI can make mistakes, so verify using Britannica articles. What role do blood vessels play in the disease process? In viral hemorrhagic fevers, blood vessels play a central role in the disease process. These diseases are caused by bloodborne viruses that damage the vascular system, leading to extensive bleeding internally, externally, and under the skin. Symptoms often include fever, fatigue, muscle aches, and exhaustion. These viruses are typically transmitted to humans via animals such as rodents and insects. There are no vaccines available, and treatment is mainly supportive. Preventing infection involves avoiding contact with host species and controlling rodent and insect populations. Isolation of infected individuals can also prevent human-to-human spread through physical contact. 2 Britannica Sources viral hemorrhagic fever bloodborne disease: Common bloodborne diseases Created from Britannica articles using AI. AI can make mistakes, so verify using Britannica articles. Why do people with these fevers sometimes bleed or bruise easily? Viral hemorrhagic fevers (VHFs) are a group of illnesses caused by bloodborne viruses that damage the vascular system. This damage leads to bleeding under the skin, in internal organs, and from body orifices. Several factors contribute to the ease of bleeding and bruising: * Vascular Damage VHFs can cause vascular damage. * Coagulation Abnormalities Viral infections can cause abnormalities in blood clotting. * Cytokine Release Unregulated cytokine production may lead to vascular damage and hemorrhaging. Some VHFs are highly fatal; certain Ebola strains have mortality rates of up to 90%. Isolation of infected individuals helps prevent the spread of VHFs, as transmission can occur through physical contact. 3 Britannica Sources viral hemorrhagic fever Marburgvirus bloodborne disease: Common bloodborne diseases Created from Britannica articles using AI. AI can make mistakes, so verify using Britannica articles. How does the body respond to fight off a viral hemorrhagic fever? Viral hemorrhagic fevers are a group of severe illnesses caused by various virus families that damage the vascular system, leading to bleeding. The body's response involves several complex mechanisms. The infection typically begins with the virus entering the body through contact with an infected animal or insect. Once inside, the virus targets cells in the vascular system, such as endothelial cells, which line blood vessels. The damage to these cells leads to increased vascular permeability and impaired blood clotting. This results in both internal and external hemorrhaging, as blood leaks from the vessels. The immune system responds by releasing cytokines, which are signaling molecules that help coordinate the immune response. However, in severe cases, this can lead to a "cytokine storm," where an excessive amount of cytokines are released, causing inflammation, shock, and organ failure. 2 Britannica Sources viral hemorrhagic fever bloodborne disease: Common bloodborne diseases Created from Britannica articles using AI. Show more Show less viral hemorrhagic fever, any of a variety of highly fatal viral diseases that are characterized by massive external or internal bleeding or bleeding into the skin. Other symptoms vary by the type of viral hemorrhagic fever but often include fever, malaise, muscle aches, vomiting, and shock. Most viral hemorrhagic fevers are geographically restricted because they are transmitted by specific animal or insect hosts (reservoirs) that occupy narrow and sometimes localized ecological niches. Viral hemorrhagic fevers are caused by viruses of four families: Flaviviridae, Arenaviridae, Bunyaviridae, and Filoviridae. The most common viral hemorrhagic fevers are dengue and yellow fever, caused by related mosquito-borne flaviviruses, often being transmitted by Aedes mosquitoes. In the late 18th century, yellow fever epidemics in American coastal cities caused widespread panic, but the disease currently occurs only in developing countries of Africa and South America. It is the only major viral hemorrhagic fever for which an effective preventive vaccine exists and is widely used. Most cases of dengue, seen in tropical areas, are mild and influenza-like, but all four dengue viruses may produce dengue hemorrhagic fever or its severe form, dengue shock syndrome. Unlike yellow fever, which affects the liver and causes severe bleeding, dengue involves the liver only minimally and tends to induce only minor bleeding that is rarely fatal. However, if dengue shock syndrome occurs, patients may die when fluids and electrolytes in their vascular compartments shift into tissues, collapsing the blood volume and precipitating low blood pressure and shock. Dengue is unique among the fatal hemorrhagic fevers in that even severe cases can be effectively treated with simple fluid administration. The arenaviruses are highly adapted to specific rodent hosts, which may become silently infected and excrete the virus in feces, urine, and saliva. However, when humans come into contact with food or soil contaminated by these rodent excreta, disease may result. The arenaviruses cause the diseases Lassa fever (occurring in Africa), Argentine hemorrhagic fever, Bolivian hemorrhagic fever, Brazilian hemorrhagic fever, and Venezuelan hemorrhagic fever. supplementary_news.content_title: 曾错过最佳时机?埃博拉疫情已超万例,为何至今仍无疫苗可用_腾讯新闻
supplementary_news.content: 本迪布焦型埃博拉仍无获批疫苗,刚果病例已超万例 现有疫苗仅针对扎伊尔型,研究发现其可引发本迪布焦交叉免疫反应 疗效尚未证实,贸然接种可能带来虚假安全感并损害公众信任 武装冲突、交通不便和追踪漏洞拖慢防控,关键瓶颈是及时响应 刚果已启动候选疫苗研究,首批可靠数据待出且投入使用至少还需数月 尽管埃博拉病毒已被人类认识数十年,但针对当前疫情的本迪布焦型病毒仍然没有可用疫苗。 然而,最新研究为预防不同类型的埃博拉带来了希望。 1976年,一种当时未知的疾病在埃博拉河附近暴发,地点是当时的扎伊尔,即今天的刚果民主共和国。这标志着埃博拉疫情首次被科学记录。 五十年后,刚果民主共和国再次成为大规模埃博拉疫情的中心。这次的病原体是埃博拉病毒属中较为少见的本迪布焦型。 该病毒于2007年在乌干达本迪布焦的一次疫情中首次被确认,2012年又在刚果民主共和国引发过一次疫情。 自5月以来,刚果的本迪布焦病例已超过一万例,最近 肯尼亚 和 尼日利亚 也报告了相关病例。 本迪布焦疫苗本可以有所准备 为何一种已被认识多年的病毒,仍能持续感染成千上万人,而至今没有获批疫苗或正式治疗手段? 杜塞尔多夫大学医院的热带医学医生托斯滕·费尔特认为,这是一个被错失的机会。 “本迪布焦病毒在2007年和2012年的疫情中曾出现过,我们本有足够的时间去开发疫苗和治疗方案,但没有抓住这个机会,结果在当前的疫情中失去了宝贵时间。”他说。 德国感染研究中心和汉堡-埃彭多夫大学医学中心的莱奥妮·迈尔也持相同看法。 “他们当然可以更早开发疫苗、开展临床前试验。”迈尔对德国之声表示。不过,她强调,疫苗的实际效果只有在真实疫情中才能得到评估和确认。 迈尔是近期一项研究的第一作者。该研究探讨的是,已获批的埃博拉疫苗Ervebo能否用于预防其他类型的 埃博拉病毒 。 为什么埃博拉是疫苗开发的理想对象 从免疫学角度看,埃博拉相比流感或HIV等病原体,更具疫苗开发价值。 流感病毒不断变异,人类免疫缺陷病毒善于逃避人体免疫防御,而埃博拉的可预测性要高得多。 迈尔表示:“也许这算是一种因祸得福——针对本迪布焦开发疫苗可能相对简单直接。” 悖论在于,尽管从科学角度看埃博拉是理想的疫苗开发对象,但本迪布焦型病毒至今没有任何获批的预防手段。 迈尔解释说,不可能针对每种潜在病原体都预先开发疫苗。资金不足或优先选择其他病原体,往往是影响因素。 此前许多研究者判断,苏丹型埃博拉病毒卷土重来的可能性更大,因此针对该型病毒的疫苗研发更为领先。 不同类型的埃博拉 问题的另一个层面在于,埃博拉并非单一病毒。已知的高危正埃博拉病毒包括埃博拉病毒(EBOV,旧称扎伊尔埃博拉病毒)、苏丹病毒(SUDV)和本迪布焦病毒(BDBV)。 现有疫苗Ervebo是针对扎伊尔型开发并获批的,对其他类型的病毒则没有获批的保护手段。 因此,现有埃博拉疫苗对当前疫区民众的作用十分有限。 另一个重要因素是,本迪布焦病毒的侵袭性似乎弱于扎伊尔型。 乍一听这是好消息,但它可能反而加大防控难度——感染者保持活动能力的时间更长,并可能在不知情的情况下传播病毒。 Ervebo疫苗显示出对本迪布焦的免疫反应 在近期发表的研究中,迈尔所在的德国感染研究中心团队考察了这款已获批疫苗能否在EBOV之外,也对其他类型的埃博拉病毒激发免疫反应。 他们发现了针对本迪布焦的交叉反应性T细胞免疫,对苏丹病毒也有程度较弱的类似反应。 对迈尔而言,这是一个重要发现。“我们现在知道,免疫细胞很可能也能识别本迪布焦病毒。”她说。 “不过我们的数据还无法回答,这种免疫反应是否真正提供保护,或者能否减轻病程。”她补充道,这是认知上的重要空白。 现有疫苗为何不能立即投入使用 既然疫苗已经获批,又有迹象表明它可能具有保护作用,为什么不直接投入使用? 迈尔解释了其中的两难。首先,在尚不确定疫苗是否有效或效果如何时投入使用,是不符合伦理的。 此外,一旦大规模使用,就无法验证它是否真的有效——病例下降可能是其他防控措施的成果,也可能是疫情本身已过峰值。 伯恩哈德·诺赫特研究所的热带病专家于尔根·迈同样反对大规模接种。“ 在没有疗效证据的情况下大规模接种,可能造成虚假的安全感,透支公众信任;而一旦它无法提供足够保护,还会让后续研究无法进行。”他说。 疫区民众的接受度同样至关重要。“如果我们大规模给人们接种疫苗,事后却发现效果远不如预期,就很难向当地人解释清楚。”迈尔说。在最坏的情况下,人们此后可能会拒绝接种那些更为有效的疫苗。 为什么埃博拉依然难以遏制 但当前疫情也表明,仅靠医学创新是不够的。 武装冲突、交通不便、针对医疗设施的袭击以及接触者追踪的漏洞,都让疫情防控难上加难。 托斯滕·费尔特表示,识别本迪布焦病毒本身已不再是难题,真正的瓶颈在于诊断手段能否实际到位。 “在偏远或受冲突影响的地区,样本常需长途运输。”他解释道。 这体现了埃博拉的另一个悖论:尽管世界诊断感染的能力越来越强,但依然难以足够快地遏制疫情。 最新一期《自然》杂志的文章作者得出同样结论:问题不在于发现病例,而在于反应速度。他们写道,如今发现埃博拉比阻止它更容易。 从本迪布焦疫苗到泛埃博拉疫苗? 许多研究者认为,当前的危机也可能是一次重要契机。 旨在测试不同候选疫苗的Tumaini研究已在刚果启动,研究对象包括牛津大学开发的Ervebo疫苗及莫德纳公司的一款mRNA疫苗。 该研究有望提供这些疫苗针对本迪布焦病毒有效性的首批可靠数据。 这些疫苗是否能帮助控制当前疫情,目前尚无定论。希望是有的,但专家估计,从现实情况看, 任何一种疫苗要投入使用至少还需数月,可能要到2027年年中。 “理想情况下,我们将开发出具有交叉保护作用的泛埃博拉疫苗。”德国感染研究中心研究的共同作者克里斯托夫·盖尔德马赫谈到长期计划时说。相关研究也在推进中。不过目前,首要任务仍是开发出针对本迪布焦型病毒的有效疫苗。 作者:汉娜·富克斯 文章仅供交流学习,不代表本号观点 本文出处:Ebola: Why is there still no vaccine?

supplementary_news.content_title: WHO adds two experimental vaccines to Ebola trial targeting deadly Bundibugyo strain
supplementary_news.content: NAIROBI,Kenya, Nov 5- The World Health Organization (WHO) has recommended the addition of two experimental vaccines specifically designed to protect against the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola to an ongoing clinical trial in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), expanding efforts to develop protection against the virus driving the current outbreak. The vaccines, ChAdOx1, developed by the University of Oxford in partnership with the Serum Institute of India, and Moderna’s mRNA-1469, are set to join the Tumaini clinical trial following national regulatory approvals. The recommendation, made this week by WHO’s independent Technical Advisory Group on Candidate Vaccines Prioritization, marks the first time vaccines specifically developed against the Bundibugyo virus will be evaluated during an outbreak of the disease. The move comes as researchers intensify efforts to establish the safety and effectiveness of vaccines against a strain for which existing Ebola vaccines have not been established to provide protection. WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said the progress demonstrated the importance of scientific collaboration and investments in vaccine development. “The fact that these vaccines are ready to enter clinical trials is a testament to the power of science and partnership,” Tedros said. He, however, cautioned that vaccination alone would not be sufficient to end the outbreak, describing vaccines as a potential additional tool in controlling the disease. The Tumaini trial, led by the DRC’s Institut National de Recherche Biomédicale (INRB), uses a ring-vaccination approach that targets contacts of people confirmed to have Bundibugyo virus disease. The approach builds on lessons from the 2014–2016 West Africa Ebola outbreak, when a landmark clinical trial in Guinea established the efficacy of Ervebo against the Zaire ebolavirus strain. Ervebo is already being evaluated in the Tumaini trial to establish its effectiveness against Bundibugyo virus, with four vaccination rings established and several others being prepared. The rings include contacts of people who have fallen ill or died from the infection. Beyond vaccine development, WHO is also supporting trials investigating potential treatments for patients infected with the virus. The PARTNERS trial, launched in July, is assessing whether the monoclonal antibody MBP134, the antiviral drug remdesivir or a combination of both can improve survival among patients with confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease. Researchers also plan to introduce maftivimab into the trial, while a separate post-exposure prophylaxis study is evaluating obeldevisir as a potential intervention for people exposed to the virus. WHO said initial findings from the treatment studies are expected in the coming months, while results from the vaccine trial are anticipated in early 2027. The research is being supported through WHO’s Research and Development Blueprint and Health Emergencies Programme, which are coordinating scientific partnerships, technical guidance and operational support to ensure studies are conducted alongside the outbreak response. The vaccine development programme has received investments from the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI), with the trial bringing together research institutions and health partners from the DRC, Belgium and other countries. The expansion of the trials is expected to generate evidence on potential vaccines and treatments against Bundibugyo virus, an Ebola strain that requires targeted research to establish effective medical countermeasures. AMCP Nexus 2026| HSES 2026 Advertisement News|Articles|November 5, 2026 WHO adds two Bundibugyo vaccines to Ebola trial in the DRC Author(s)Briana Contreras WHO advisers backed adding Oxford/Serum Institute of India and Moderna vaccine candidates to the Tumaini trial against the Bundibugyo Ebola strain. Advertisement Two experimental vaccines made to fight a type of Ebola virus that is behind the outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) will be added to the country's Tumaini clinical trial, the World Health Organization (WHO) said in a recent news release. The vaccines—ChAdOx1 BDBV, which comes from the University of Oxford and the Serum Institute of India, and Moderna's mRNA-1469—were added to combat Bundibugyo. A WHO advisory group recommended both vaccines for more testing this week, based on lab, animal and early human data. They will join the trial once national approvals are in place. WHO said this is the first time vaccines built for the Bundibugyo virus will be tested during an outbreak. “Vaccines alone will not end this outbreak, but they could become a powerful new tool for bringing it under control,” Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, Ph.D., WHO director-general, said in the release. What is Bundibugyo virus disease? Three viruses are known to cause large Ebola outbreaks: Ebola virus (often called the Zaire type), Sudan virus and Bundibugyo virus, according to the WHO Ebola fact sheet. Fruit bats are thought to carry the viruses in nature. People catch it through direct contact with an infected person's blood or body fluids, or with surfaces those fluids have touched. People can't spread it before they have symptoms. Symptoms show up 2 to 21 days after infection and often start suddenly. Early signs include fever, fatigue, muscle pain and headache. After, patients may have vomiting, diarrhea, rash and kidney and liver problems. On average, about half of people with Ebola die, WHO says, though past outbreaks have ranged from 25% to 90%. Bundibugyo virus was first found in 2007 in the Bundibugyo district of western Uganda. A second outbreak hit the DRC in 2012, according to the UK Health Security Agency. The current outbreak began in May. It is now the largest Bundibugyo outbreak on record and the second-largest Ebola outbreak ever. As of late October, the DRC had reported 10,193 confirmed cases and 4,960 deaths across eight provinces, according to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC). Cases tied to the outbreak have also turned up in Kenya and Nigeria. According to the release, there is a major gap in tools to fight it. The approved Ebola vaccines—Ervebo (Ebola Zaire vaccine) and the two-dose Zabdeno (Ad26.ZEBOV) and Mvabea (MVA-BN-Filo) regimen—work only against the Zaire type. The same is true of the two approved antibody treatments, Ebanga (ansuvimab-zykl) and Inmazeb (atoltivimab, maftivimab and odesivimab-ebgn). How the Tumaini Ebola vaccine trial works Meaning "hope" in Swahili, the Tumaini phase 2/3 trial gave its first shot in late October in Bunia, the capital of Ituri province and the center of the outbreak, the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI) said in a news release. Ervebo was the first vaccine tested to see whether it also protects against Bundibugyo. The trial can test several vaccines under one plan. It uses ring vaccination, which means vaccinating the contacts of people with confirmed cases. A similar trial in Guinea about a decade ago proved Ervebo worked against the Zaire type. Four vaccination rings are in place, and more are being set up. The DRC's Institut National de Recherche Biomédicale and Belgium's University of Antwerp lead the trial. WHO, Médecins Sans Frontières and other groups are partners, and CEPI is funding vaccine development. “There is still no licensed vaccine against Bundibugyo virus, and the cost of that absence is being counted in the DRC every day, in lives lost and in health workers who go to work without protection” Richard Hatchett, M.D., CEO of CEPI, said when the trial launched. Treatment research for Bundibugyo virus disease Researchers are also testing treatments. The WHO-sponsored PARTNERS trial, which began in July, is studying whether patients are more likely to survive if they get the experimental antibody MBP134, the antiviral Veklury (remdesivir) or both. Maftivimab, one of the three antibodies in Inmazeb, will soon be added to the trial. A separate study, EBO-PEP, is testing whether an experimental antiviral pill, obeldesivir, can keep high-risk contacts from getting sick. Early results from the treatment trial are expected in the coming months, and vaccine results are expected in early 2027, WHO said. Tedros called the vaccines' readiness for testing “a testament to the power of science and partnership.” Newsletter Get the latest industry news, event updates and more from Managed Healthcare Executive.
