supplementary_news.content_title: Two New Ebola Vaccine Candidates Recommended Amidst DRC Outbreak
supplementary_news.content: TWO NEW vaccine candidates for the Bundibugyo Ebola virus have been recommended for clinical evaluation as the outbreak of the disease continues to spread and claim lives in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC). Announced by the World Health Organization (WHO), the recommendation will mark the first time vaccines developed specifically against the Bundibugyo strain of the virus are tested during an active outbreak. The candidates will join the ongoing Tumaini trial following national approvals. Two New Candidates for Clinical Evaluation. The candidates, ChAdOx1, developed by the University of Oxford with the Serum Institute of India, and Moderna’s mRNA-1469, will join the ongoing Tumaini vaccine trial in DRC if granted national approval. Using a ring-vaccination approach, the trial enrols contacts of people with confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease. Four vaccination rings are already established, with more being prepared. WHO’s independent Technical Advisory Group on Candidate Vaccine Prioritization recommended both for further evaluation based on preclinical and early clinical evidence. Their inclusion mark a promising step forward in research aiming to tackle the current disease outbreak in DRC which has already claimed the lives of over 5,000 people. Ervebo, an already established vaccine which has demonstrated efficacy against Zaire strain of the ebolavirus is already being evaluated in Tumaini to assess whether it also protects against Bundibugyo virus. Continuing Transmission and Loss of Life. The research developments come as the outbreak continues to place pressure on affected communities. According to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control (ECDC), as of November, the DRC had reported 10,532 confirmed cases of the disease in total, including 5,126 deaths. Eight provinces in the country have been affected, with Ituri and North Kivu accounting for the greatest burden. Cases have also been reported in Kenya and Nigeria, although reports at the beginning of the month showed no new recorded cases since a previous weekly updare. Uganda’s outbreak was declared over in August. Insecurity and ongoing humanitarian challenges in the region also limit understanding of patterns of spread and have in some instances curbed efforts to stop transmission,. The ECDC cautions that reported figures remain subject to review and reconciliation and that the outbreak could potentially be larger than detected. Treatment Research Advances. Alongside vaccination research, the WHO-sponsored PARTNERS trial is investigating whether the monoclonal antibody MBP134, the antiviral remdesivir, or their combination can improve survival in patients already infected with the virus. Maftivimab, which is currently one part of an approved three part monoclonal antibody fixed-dose drug cocktail for Zaire ebolavirus, is also expected to be added to the trial. A further complementary study is also evaluating obeldevisir, a nucleoside anti-viral agent, as post-exposure prophylaxis. Initial treatment findings are expected in the coming months, with vaccine-trial results anticipated in early 2027. WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus welcomed the progress, hailing the vaccines “a powerful new tool” and a “ testament to the power of science and partnership,” but stressed that “vaccines alone will not end this outbreak”. European Response and Preparedness. European involvement extends beyond vaccine development. ECDC experts have supported epidemiological work in the DRC and preparedness and response activities in Nigeria. Although patients with the infection have been medically evacuated or imported into European countries, ECDC continues to assess the likelihood of infection among people living in the EU/EEA as very low. The immediate challenge remains controlling transmission in affected areas while generating evidence on interventions that could prevent illness and improve survival. These two new vaccine candidates are certainly a step in this direction. Feautre image: MargJohnsonVA on AdobeStock. Author: Cecilia Adamou

supplementary_news.content: English Login Homepage Topic News Political System Destination Event Travel Happy Vietnam Enterprise Product Heritage Museum Figure Multimedia Data Home News World The "war" against Ebola: The world's test for future pandemics. ANTD.VN - The developments during the Ebola outbreak in eastern Congo have exposed growing gaps in the global health security system, including the research and development of vaccines against this dangerous disease. Tìm hiểu lịch sử Báo An ninh Thủ đô•10/11/2026 Follow Vietnam.vn on Google Add Vietnam.vn on Google 0 The Ebola epidemic had a profound impact on children in the Democratic Republic of Congo. There is no vaccine specifically for the Bundibugyo strain. Half a century after the Ebola virus was discovered and more than six months after the outbreak intensified in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), the world still lacks a licensed vaccine against the Bundibugyo strain – the causative agent of the current outbreak. Since the World Health Organization (WHO) declared the Ebola outbreak in Congo a public health emergency of international concern on May 17th, more than 10,000 cases have been confirmed, including 4,887 deaths, representing a mortality rate of 48.6%. Khám phá thêm Tìm hiểu lịch sử Đọc Mẹo Du Lịch Khám phá ĐNA Ebola, also known as Ebola hemorrhagic fever, is a deadly disease caused by the Ebola virus. Initially, the Ebola virus was found in monkeys, chimpanzees, and other primates in Africa. Another strain of Ebola has also been detected in monkeys and pigs in the Philippines . Many experts believe that the Ebola virus is transmitted from animals to humans through the bodily fluids of infected animals, such as blood, feces, and urine. People who slaughter or eat infected animals are at a high risk of infection, as is contact with the feces or urine of cave-dwelling bats. Between people, the Ebola virus is transmitted through direct contact with the blood, vomit, urine, and other bodily fluids of infected individuals, those who have died from Ebola, or infected animals. Objects and surfaces contaminated with the body fluids of infected individuals, such as clothing and bedding, can also transmit the disease. Once inside the body, the Ebola virus damages the immune system and other organs, reduces blood clotting ability, and causes severe and uncontrollable bleeding (hemorrhage). The mortality rate from Ebola infection is very high, ranging from 50% to 90% of infected individuals. The Ebola virus is divided into five main subgroups: Zaire, Sudan, Bundibugyo, Tai Forest Ebolavirus (formerly known as Côte d'Ivoire), and Reston, each named after the location where it was first discovered. Of these, the Zaire subgroup has a significantly higher mortality rate than the others, with a rate of 40-60% compared to Sudan and approximately 25% compared to Bundibugyo. Over the past decade, the world has made significant progress in controlling Ebola, particularly with the more prevalent Zaire strain. Vaccines, gene sequencing technology, rapid testing, and experience gained in Africa have helped many countries control outbreaks more quickly than during the 2014-2016 West African Ebola crisis. However, currently only the Ervebo vaccine is licensed to protect against the Zaire strain of Ebola. Meanwhile, the current Ebola outbreak in Congo is linked to the rare Bundibugyo strain, for which there is no vaccine. Because it is considered relatively rare, the Bundibugyo strain is not a top priority for pharmaceutical companies to focus research on. Therefore, when an outbreak occurs, the world almost has to start from scratch. You may also like Medical personnel are carrying out disinfection in an infected area in Congo. The complex security situation in eastern Congo is increasing the risk of disease spread. Many areas in North Kivu and South Kivu are currently under the control of armed groups, while poor infrastructure hinders the transport of aid workers and medical supplies. The outbreak is occurring amidst a surge in armed conflict and displacement of refugees in the region. This context has led the WHO to express particular concern about gaps in epidemiological surveillance, testing capacity, prevention, and emergency response in countries with already strained healthcare systems. Furthermore, recent cuts in international aid have scaled back many Ebola surveillance and prevention programs in eastern Congo. Some humanitarian organizations have been forced to reduce their operations due to a lack of funding for protective equipment and medical personnel. Many experts warn that budget cuts for vaccine research, disease surveillance, and emergency response capabilities could leave the world more vulnerable to new health threats. Strengthening public health in disease control The race to combat Ebola Bundibugyo is now not only a scientific challenge, but also a test of the world's preparedness for future pandemics. Researchers are currently working to adapt existing vaccine technologies to combat the Bundibugyo strain. This is seen as a faster solution because it can leverage existing scientific and technological foundations. In principle, this approach is similar to the Covid-19 vaccines that used spike proteins to "train" the immune system to recognize the virus. However, despite the promising idea, producing a clinically-grade vaccine still takes many months, not to mention the safety and efficacy testing phases in animals and humans. Another approach is to utilize mRNA technology – the foundation that revolutionized vaccines during the Covid-19 pandemic. This technology has the advantage of rapid development and easy adaptation to new viral variants. Several collaborative projects between European universities and major biotechnology companies have been launched to research mRNA vaccines against Bundibugyo. However, experts acknowledge that there is still a long way to go from the laboratory to practical implementation. While a specific vaccine is not yet available, some scientists are considering a "temporary" solution: using existing Ebola vaccines to create cross-protection. This idea is based on the hypothesis that the immune system activated by the Ebola Zaire vaccine may partially recognize and prevent the Bundibugyo strain. Some animal trials have yielded limited results, but given the current emergency, researchers want to leverage this outbreak to assess its effectiveness in humans. You may also like While awaiting trials of new vaccines, the WHO emphasizes that the current priority remains preventing the spread of Ebola through traditional measures such as disease surveillance, rapid testing, contact tracing, isolation and treatment, infection control, and safe burial. According to experts, the Bundibugyo strain, which caused two previous outbreaks in the Congo River basin, is transmitted through direct contact with the bodily fluids of infected or deceased individuals, placing healthcare workers and caregivers at the highest risk. In the absence of a specific drug or vaccine, the primary treatment currently focuses on supportive care, including hydration, medical monitoring, and isolation of patients. Current disease control measures concentrate on contact tracing, isolating cases, rapid testing, public awareness campaigns, and ensuring safe burial practices. Experts believe that despite the lack of a vaccine, traditional public health measures can still help control the epidemic. Another issue requiring attention is strengthening international cooperation, especially increasing investment in global health. According to statistics, total global development aid for health is projected to fall to approximately $39 billion in 2025, the lowest level in over 15 years, and is forecast to further decrease to $36 billion by 2030. The main reason is that donor countries are shifting their budget priorities, focusing resources on other issues, including economic recovery. Experts believe that cuts in foreign aid could cause a shock on a scale equivalent to "a global pandemic or a major armed conflict" for many low- and middle-income countries, leading to serious consequences. Strengthening the resilience of global health systems depends heavily on the determination of each country and region to harness its potential, while also requiring continuous, close, transparent cooperation and a rapid response from the international community. Trial in DR Congo BrandIconImage a day ago The World Health Organisation (WHO) has recommended two additional vaccine candidates for an ongoing Ebola clinical trial in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), raising hopes for improved efforts to contain outbreaks caused by the Bundibugyo virus. The recommendation marks a significant development in the fight against the disease, as the vaccines are specifically designed to provide protection against the Bundibugyo virus, a strain for which no approved vaccine is currently available. The two candidates are ChAdOx1, developed by the University of Oxford in collaboration with the Serum Institute of India, and mRNA-1469, developed by American biotechnology company Moderna. Their selection followed an assessment of available preclinical and early clinical evidence by WHO's Independent Technical Advisory Group on Candidate Vaccines Prioritisation. The vaccines are expected to join the ongoing Tumaini clinical trial, which evaluates multiple vaccine candidates within a single study using a ring-vaccination strategy. Under this approach, individuals who have come into contact with confirmed cases of Bundibugyo virus disease are vaccinated to determine how effectively the vaccines can prevent further transmission. The trial is being led by the DRC's Institut National de Recherche Biomédicale, in collaboration with the University of Antwerp and international partners, including WHO, Médecins Sans Frontières and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention. The Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations has also supported efforts towards the rapid development of the vaccine candidates. The Tumaini study builds on the ring-vaccination strategy deployed during the West African Ebola outbreak, which helped establish the effectiveness of Ervebo against the Zaire ebolavirus. Ervebo is already being assessed as part of the ongoing trial to determine its potential effectiveness against the Bundibugyo virus. According to WHO, four vaccination rings have already been established, with additional rings being prepared as the study progresses. WHO Director-General, Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus, described the development as an important demonstration of scientific collaboration and international efforts to strengthen preparedness against infectious disease outbreaks. He expressed optimism that the additional vaccine candidates could provide another important tool for controlling the outbreak and protecting vulnerable populations. NCDC, German Institute Strengthen AMR Surveillance Meanwhile, efforts to tackle antimicrobial resistance (AMR) in Nigeria have received renewed attention, as the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC), in partnership with Germany's Robert Koch Institute, convened a two-day stakeholder dialogue in Abuja to strengthen the country's surveillance system. The engagement, organised under the NiCaDe AMR Project, brought together representatives of sentinel laboratories, healthcare institutions, academic organisations and development partners to examine existing surveillance structures and identify practical ways to improve the monitoring and response to antimicrobial resistance. Participants reviewed a decade of AMR surveillance data, assessed operational challenges and discussed measures to strengthen the country's capacity to detect, monitor and respond to drug-resistant infections. In a post on X, the NCDC said discussions centred on improving laboratory capacity, strengthening data quality, promoting institutional mentorship and encouraging greater collaboration across different levels of the healthcare system. The dialogue also examined the importance of diagnostic stewardship and the responsible use of antimicrobial medicines, which are essential to reducing the emergence and spread of drug-resistant infections. As part of the discussions, stakeholders identified priority actions to guide the development of a national Hub-and-Spoke framework for strengthening AMR surveillance and antimicrobial stewardship across the country. The proposed framework is expected to improve coordination between laboratories and healthcare institutions, enhance the collection and sharing of reliable surveillance data, and support evidence-based decisions on patient treatment. The approach is also expected to strengthen the country's ability to identify emerging resistance patterns and provide healthcare professionals with more reliable information when selecting appropriate antimicrobial treatments. The NCDC reaffirmed its commitment to building a stronger evidence base for treatment decisions, improving surveillance capacity and supporting coordinated national efforts to address the growing threat of antimicrobial resistance. The twin developments highlight the importance of scientific research, international partnerships and stronger public health systems in addressing emerging infectious diseases and protecting access to effective treatments. OffOn Stream on Ebola outbreak sees 136 suspected deaths in DRC, officials say More than 40 health experts were deployed to the field on Sunday. ByMorgan Winsor, David Brennan, Dr. Geraldine Nabeta, Othon Leyva, and Mary Kekatos May 20, 2026, 1:39 AM Share At least 543 suspected cases and 136 suspected deaths have been recorded in the ongoing Ebola outbreak in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo, officials said Tuesday. Congolese Minister of Public Health Samuel Roger Kamba said during a press briefing that authorities will determine which of these deaths "are actually linked to the disease." At least 30 cases of Ebola have been confirmed in Congo, officials said. Cases have been reported in urban areas, including one of Congo's largest cities, Goma, the rebel-held capital of the eastern province of North Kivu, according to World Health Organization Director-General Dr. Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus. Uganda has also confirmed two cases in its capital Kampala, including one death, among two individuals who traveled from neighboring Congo, according to Tedros. A visitor washes his hands before entering Kyeshero Hospital at a checkpoint in Goma, Democratic Republic of Congo, on May 18, 2026. Jospin Mwisha/AFP via Getty Images During the WHO's annual World Health Assembly in Geneva on Tuesday, Tedros said he is "deeply concerned" about the outbreak while explaining why he declared a public health emergency of international concern in connection with the Ebola cases in Congo and neighboring Uganda. "I did not do this lightly," Tedros said. "I did it in accordance with Article 12 of the International Health Regulations, after consulting the ministers of health of both countries, and because I am deeply concerned about the scale and speed of the epidemic. We will convene the Emergency Committee today to advise us on temporary recommendations." The outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo virus, a rare variant of Ebola for which there are no approved vaccines or therapeutics, Tedros said. According to The Associated Press, more than 20 Ebola outbreaks have occurred in Congo and Uganda, but this is only the third time that the Bundibugyo virus has been detected. Health officials in Uganda say they feel "very confident" in dealing with the epidemic. "We have built capacity in the country. We have built the human capital and the skill. We have infrastructure," Dr. Diana Atwine, who serves as the acting health minister for Uganda, told ABC News on Tuesday. "We have very strong surveillance teams. That's what we do best." Health officials in Uganda are working at border checkpoints to ensure any incoming travelers are screened for potential illness, she said. Testing sites and diagnostic laboratories have also been activated to support the public health response. The State Department said Tuesday it was launching a Disaster Assistance Response Team (DART) to address the outbreak, according to a department official. Members of the team were headed to Kinshasa in Congo and Kampala in Uganda, according to the official. The department said it would also fund up to 50 clinics in Ebola-affected regions of Congo and Uganda that will provide emergency screening, triage and isolation capacity. These clinics will be run by government partners and primarily funded through contributions the U.S. has already provided to the United Nations. Related American doctor tests positive for Ebola in Democratic Republic of Congo outbreak Dr. Anne Ancia, WHO's representative in the DRC, said Tuesday that more than 40 experts were deployed to the field on Sunday. The WHO has sent 12 tons of supplies so far -- including personal protective equipment for frontline healthcare workers, laboratory samples, tents, drugs and other treatments -- with six more tons coming, she said. "What I see here in the field is extremely vulnerable people, a [fragile] population," Ancia said. "But I see also people working together while facing great uncertainty as to the [scale] or the extent of this outbreak." She said the surveillance capacity is limited in the affected region, which could be why the outbreak is spreading rapidly. "We really need to go fast to really try to stop the spread of the disease further," she said. "We don't understand yet the extent of the spread of the disease." Dr. Peter Stafford, a medical missionary with the missions organization Serge, was exposed while treating patients at Nyankunde Hospital, the group said Monday. He sought testing "after presenting symptoms consistent with the virus," Serge said in a statement. Fatima Tafida, the Regional Supply Chain Lead for Emergencies at the World Health Organization's Regional Office for Africa, pastes stickers on shipment pallets at an airport in in Nairobi, Kenya, on May 18, 2026. World Health Organization/via Reuters Dr. Scott Myhre, a colleague of Stafford, said the doctor was exposed to Ebola during surgery on a "very sick" patient who later died. Scott said Stafford developed symptoms that can resemble other diseases including fever, aches, chills and fatigue -- which can make Ebola difficult to diagnose and treat. Stafford has since received IV fluids and was put on a biocontamination plane Tuesday morning to a U.S. military base in Germany, Scott said. He added that Stafford was put on the plane in a plastic bubble-like contraption to avoid exposing others traveling with him. Other high-risk contacts, including Stafford's wife and children, are being monitored in quarantine and are expected to be flown to Germany on Wednesday, according to Scott. Dr. Satish K. Pillai, incident manager for the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's Ebola response, confirmed at a CDC press conference on Tuesday that six other high-risk contacts "are also having movement plans that are finalizing and will be transiting to Europe as well shortly." He added that genetic testing from this outbreak shows it is similar to the "genetic fingerprints" from outbreaks in 2007 and 2012, meaning there are diagnostic tools available that can detect this strain of Ebola. Related 'We’re working on it': HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on Ebola, hantavirus response Pillai said on Monday that the agency had activated its Emergency Operations Center through its country offices in the DRC and in Uganda, and is deploying technical experts that have been requested from Atlanta headquarters. The CDC said Monday that it is preparing to restrict entry for travelers arriving from parts of central Africa where an Ebola outbreak has been declared, in coordination with the Department of Homeland Security. The risk to the U.S. general public remains low, Pillai said. ABC News' Youri Benadjaoud, Eric M. Strauss and Mary Kekatos contributed to this report. Facebook Twitter WhatsApp Flipboard LinkedIn Reddit Email Share Dany Bitita/WHO Two new candidate vaccines to join Ebola trial as treatment research advances. 7 November 2026 Deutsche Welle (Bonn) By Hannah Fuchs Ebola has been known about for decades, but there is still no vaccine against the Bundibugyo strain of the virus causing the current outbreak. New research raises hopes of protection against the various types of Ebola. 1976: A hitherto unknown disease breaks out near the Ebola river in the country then known as Zaire, now the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). This was the first scientifically documented Ebola epidemic. Now, 50 years on, the DRC once again finds itself at the center of a major Ebola outbreak. This time the pathogen is the less common Bundibugyo type of the genus orthoebolavirus. The virus was identified in 2007 during an outbreak in Bundibugyo, Uganda. Another outbreak occurred in the DRC in 2012. Preparations could have been made for Bundibugyo Follow us on WhatsApp | LinkedIn for the latest headlines How can a virus that has been known for decades continue to infect thousands of people, yet there is still no licensed vaccine or official treatment? Torsten Feldt, a doctor of tropical medicine at Düsseldorf's University Hospital, sees this as a missed opportunity. "We had come across the Bundibugyo virus in two previous outbreaks: 2007 in Uganda and 2012 in DR Congo. So we had enough time to develop vaccines and therapeutic options. But we didn't make use of this opportunity, meaning crucial time was lost during the current outbreak," he said. Leonie Mayer from the German Center for Infection Research (DZIF) and the Institute for Infection Research and Vaccine Development at the University Medical Center in Hamburg-Eppendorf agrees. "They could of course have developed a vaccine and run pre-clinical trials before," Mayer told DW. She stressed, however, that their effectiveness can only be assessed and confirmed during an actual outbreak. Mayer is the lead author of a recently published study that examined whether Ervebo, an Ebola vaccine that has already been licensed, can be used against other types of Ebola as well. Why Ebola is a good candidate for vaccine development From an immunological point of view, and compared to — for example — influenza or HIV, Ebola is a very worthwhile candidate for a vaccine. Influenza viruses are constantly mutating, and the human immunodeficiency virus is particularly good at evading our immune defenses. Ebola is far more predictable. "I think — and perhaps it's kind of a blessing in disguise — that it will be relatively straightforward to develop a vaccine against Bundibugyo," said Mayer. Herein lies the paradox. From a scientific point of view, Ebola is a good vaccine candidate, yet there is still no licensed form of prevention against the Bundibugyo variant that is currently circulating. Mayer explained that vaccines cannot be developed as a precautionary measure against every potential pathogen. Lack of funding or the prioritization of other pathogens often have a role to play. Many researchers had assumed that a fresh outbreak of the Sudan Ebola virus was more likely, and vaccine development for this strain is more advanced. Different types of Ebola Another part of the problem is that Ebola is not one single virus. The known, highly dangerous orthoebolaviruses include Ebola virus (EBOV), previously called the Zaire Ebola virus (ZEBOV), the Sudan virus (SUDV), and the Bundibugyo virus (BDBV). The existing vaccine, Ervebo, was developed and licensed for use against the Zaire variant. But there is still no approved protection against the others. This is why the existing Ebola vaccine has been of only limited use to people in the areas of the current outbreak. Another factor may also be relevant: The Bundibugyo virus appears to be less aggressive than the Zaire variant. At first, that sounds like good news, but it may make it harder to contain, as people remain mobile for longer after being infected, and can pass on the virus without realizing. Ervebo vaccine shows immune response to Bundibugyo In the recently published study, Mayer's research team from the DZIF investigated whether the already licensed Ebola vaccine could trigger an immune response not only against EBOV, but against other types of Ebola as well. They found cross-reactive T-cell responses against Bundibugyo, and also, to a lesser extent, against the Sudan virus. For Mayer, this is already an important finding. "We now know that the immune cells can most likely also recognize the Bundibugyo virus," she said. "Our data does not enable us to answer the question of whether this immune response actually provides protection, or if it results in a milder progression of the disease," she added, calling it an important gap in our knowledge. Why can't existing vaccine be deployed yet? If there's a vaccine that has already been licensed, and indications that it could protect people, why isn't it simply being deployed? Mayer explains the dilemma. For one thing, she said, it's not ethical to deploy a vaccine if you're not sure whether or how well it works. Also, if it were used on a large scale, it would no longer be possible to establish whether it actually works: A reduction in cases could also be a result of other measures, or the epidemic might already have passed its peak. Jürgen May, a specialist in tropical diseases at the Bernhard Nocht Institute, also warns against mass vaccination. "Mass vaccination without proof of efficacy could create a false sense of security, forfeit trust, and, if it does not provide sufficient protection, make study impossible," he said. It's very important for there to be acceptance on the ground. "If we inoculate people with a vaccine on a large scale, and afterwards it turns out that it was nothing like as effective as we expected, it's very difficult to communicate that to people on the ground," Mayer said. In a worst-case scenario, people could subsequently refuse inoculation with more effective vaccines. Why Ebola is still so difficult to contain But the current outbreak also shows that medical innovation alone is not enough. Conflicts, difficult transport routes, attacks on healthcare facilities and gaps in contact tracing all make it harder to contain. Torsten Feldt said identifying Bundibugyo is no longer a problem in itself. What is often limiting is the practical availability of diagnostic tools. "In remote or conflict-affected regions, samples often have to be transported over long distances," he explained. Success! Almost finished... We need to confirm your email address. To complete the process, please follow the instructions in the email we just sent you. Error! Error! There was a problem processing your submission. Please try again later. Here we see another Ebola paradox. The world is getting ever better at diagnosing infections, but it still struggles to contain outbreaks fast enough. The authors of an article in the current issue of Nature come to the same conclusion: The problem is often not identifying cases, but the speed with which people react. Finding Ebola is often easier now than stopping Ebola, they wrote. From a Bundibugyo vaccine to a pan-Ebola one? Many researchers believe the current crisis could potentially also provide a great opportunity. The so-called Tumaini study, which is testing different vaccine candidates, has now been launched in Congo. These include Ervebo, developed by Oxford University, and a Moderna mRNA vaccine. The study aims to provide the first reliable data about their efficacy against the Bundibugyo virus. Whether these vaccines could still help control the current outbreak is uncertain. There is hope, but experts estimate that, realistically, it will be several months before any such vaccine is available for widespread use; perhaps not until mid-2027. "Ideally, we will develop cross-reactive pan-Ebola vaccines," Christof Geldmacher, a co-author of the DZIF study, said of their long-term plans. This is also something that is being worked on. For now, though, the focus is on developing an effective vaccine against the Bundibugyo variant of the virus. This article was originally written in German. supplementary_news.content: News Technology Business Entertainment Science & Health Knowledge Base Font ResizerAa Search News Technology Business Entertainment Science & Health Knowledge Base Follow US WHO Recommends Oxford and Moderna Vaccine Candidates for Bundibugyo Trial Last updated: November 6, 2026 1:01 am By Pam Belluck Science & Health 5 Min Read SHARE The World Health Organization has recommended two candidate vaccines for evaluation in the Tumaini clinical trial in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, subject to national approvals. No efficacy results from the trial have been reported. The recommendations concern ChAdOx1, developed by the University of Oxford and the Serum Institute of India, and Moderna’s mRNA-1469. If they enter the study, WHO says they would be the first vaccines specifically designed for Bundibugyo virus to be evaluated during an outbreak of that disease. Table of Contents Outbreak trial seeks answers beyond existing Ebola vaccine evidence Moderna candidate has begun an earlier safety study Treatment research is running alongside vaccine work Outbreak trial seeks answers beyond existing Ebola vaccine evidence “Ebola” is often used as a broad label, but it encompasses several related viruses. The distinction is crucial for vaccine research. Ervebo, a vaccine already being evaluated in Tumaini, produced landmark evidence of effectiveness against Zaire ebolavirus during the West Africa epidemic. That evidence does not establish protection against Bundibugyo virus, the virus involved in the current Congolese outbreak. WHO’s independent Technical Advisory Group on Candidate Vaccines Prioritization recommended the two additions for further clinical evaluation. Tumaini is led by the Democratic Republic of the Congo’s Institut National de Recherche Biomédicale and uses a ring-vaccination design, enrolling contacts of people with confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease. WHO says four rings are already in place and more are being prepared. Tumaini uses ring vaccination, enrolling contacts of people with confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease; WHO has not published the trial’s detailed protocol. WHO’s announcement does not provide Tumaini’s enrollment targets, statistical analysis plan or criteria for judging vaccine performance. WHO expects vaccine-trial results in early 2027. Until then, it is not known whether ChAdOx1, mRNA-1469 or Ervebo reduces Bundibugyo infections in the study population. Moderna candidate has begun an earlier safety study Moderna’s proposed participation in Tumaini follows a separate first-in-human study, not an efficacy result. In August, Reuters reported that the company had begun a Phase 1 trial of mRNA-1469 at three Canadian sites. The study was designed to enroll about 80 healthy adults and assess safety and immune responses. That Canadian trial and Tumaini address different questions. Early-phase studies in healthy volunteers are generally intended to identify safety concerns and measure biological responses, such as antibodies. An outbreak-based study is needed to assess whether vaccination is associated with fewer cases under conditions of actual virus exposure. An immune response can support continued development, but it is not by itself proof of clinical protection. Earlier coverage identified three Bundibugyo-focused candidates receiving accelerated development support: ChAdOx1, mRNA-1469 and an IAVI-associated candidate. Texas Public Radio’s report on NPR’s coverage described the three candidates. WHO’s later announcement names the two candidates recommended for Tumaini and notes that Ervebo is already under evaluation there; it does not describe the IAVI candidate’s status in this trial. Treatment research is running alongside vaccine work The vaccine study is one part of a wider clinical-research program during the outbreak. WHO says the PARTNERS treatment trial, launched in July, is testing the monoclonal-antibody candidate MBP134, the antiviral remdesivir and a combination of the two in people with confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease. These studies serve different purposes. Tumaini is designed to examine whether vaccines can prevent disease among contacts of confirmed patients. PARTNERS examines treatment options after a person has confirmed illness, with the aim of generating evidence about clinical outcomes. WHO says maftivimab is planned for addition to the treatment trial. A third research track is studying obeldevisir as post-exposure prophylaxis, meaning it is being assessed after a possible exposure but before confirmed disease. WHO expects initial treatment findings in the coming months, while vaccine-trial results are expected in early 2027. WHO’s recommendation creates a potential route for ChAdOx1 and mRNA-1469 to be evaluated in Tumaini after national approval. It does not establish that either candidate, or Ervebo, protects against Bundibugyo virus. She has reported extensively on topics like reproductive health, long-term illness, brain science, and public health, with a focus on both complex medical developments and human-centered narratives. Her writing bridges investigative depth with accessible storytelling, often covering issues at the intersection of science, ethics, and personal experience. Devdiscourse News Desk | Geneva | Updated: 09-11-2026 12:59 IST | Created: 09-11-2026 12:59 IST Scientists are investigating possible treatments for people who have contracted Bundibugyo virus disease through the WHO-sponsored PARTNERS clinical trial, launched in July 2026. Image Credit: ChatGPT SHARE Key Takeaways AI Summary Analyzing article... Two experimental Ebola vaccines designed to protect against Bundibugyo virus could soon be tested during an active outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), following recommendations from expert groups convened by the World Health Organization (WHO). The vaccines are expected to join the ongoing Tumaini clinical trial once national authorities approve their inclusion, creating the first opportunity to evaluate vaccines specifically developed for Bundibugyo virus during an outbreak. Researchers hope the findings will help identify new ways to protect communities exposed to the virus and strengthen future responses to similar health emergencies. The two vaccine candidates are ChAdOx1, developed by the University of Oxford in partnership with the Serum Institute of India, and Moderna's mRNA-1469, which uses messenger RNA technology. WHO's independent Technical Advisory Group on Candidate Vaccines Prioritization recommended both vaccines for further clinical evaluation after reviewing available laboratory research and early clinical evidence. Their inclusion in the trial represents an important development in efforts to understand whether these vaccines can provide effective protection against Bundibugyo virus disease. WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus described the progress as an example of what scientific cooperation can achieve, recognising the contributions of researchers, healthcare workers, international partners and people participating in the trial. He emphasised that vaccines alone cannot end the outbreak, but successful candidates could provide health authorities with another valuable tool to reduce infections and protect vulnerable communities. The participation of people exposed to the virus will help researchers gather evidence needed to understand vaccine effectiveness and guide future public health decisions. New Vaccines Bring Hope for Stronger Ebola Protection The Tumaini vaccine trial is being led by the DRC's Institut National de Recherche Biomédicale (INRB), working closely with Belgium's University of Antwerp and several international health organisations. Partners include WHO, Epicentre, Médecins Sans Frontières, the Institute of Tropical Medicine in Antwerp, Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention, the DRC Ministry of Health and the country's Institut National de Santé Publique. Investments from the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI) have supported the rapid development of vaccine candidates, helping researchers prepare potential protective tools for outbreaks involving different Ebola viruses. The trial allows researchers to evaluate multiple vaccine candidates within a single research programme, making it possible to gather evidence about different approaches to preventing Bundibugyo virus disease. Oxford's ChAdOx1 and Moderna's mRNA-1469 will enter the programme only after the necessary national approvals have been granted, and the required clinical arrangements are completed. Studying these vaccines during an outbreak could provide valuable information about their performance in real-world conditions, including whether they can reduce the risk of illness among people exposed to infected individuals. How Ring Vaccination Could Help Control the Outbreak The Tumaini trial follows a ring-vaccination approach, which involves identifying people who have been in contact with someone diagnosed with Bundibugyo virus disease and enrolling eligible contacts in the research. Four vaccination rings have been established, with additional groups being prepared to include contacts of people who became ill or died from Ebola. This approach allows researchers to study vaccine effectiveness among people with known exposure risks and could provide useful evidence for improving outbreak responses. The strategy draws on experience from the Ebola outbreak in West Africa about a decade ago, when WHO and its partners conducted a major vaccine trial in Guinea. That research demonstrated the effectiveness of Ervebo against Ebola virus, commonly known as Zaire ebolavirus, and helped establish ring vaccination as an important research approach during outbreaks. Ervebo is the first vaccine being evaluated in the current Tumaini trial to determine whether it offers protection against Bundibugyo virus, with the two newly recommended candidates expected to expand the research once approved. New Treatment Research Could Improve Patient Survival Scientists are investigating possible treatments for people who have contracted Bundibugyo virus disease through the WHO-sponsored PARTNERS clinical trial, launched in July 2026. The research is examining whether the monoclonal antibody MBP134, the antiviral medicine remdesivir or a combination of both can improve survival among patients with confirmed infections. Another treatment called maftivimab is expected to enter the trial, and a separate study is evaluating obeldevisir as a possible preventive medicine after exposure to the virus. WHO is supporting these studies through its Research and Development Blueprint and Health Emergencies Programme, helping researchers develop protocols, coordinate partnerships and conduct scientifically rigorous and ethical research during the outbreak. Initial findings from the treatment trials are expected in the coming months, with results from the Tumaini vaccine trial anticipated in early 2027. The research could improve understanding of how Bundibugyo virus disease can be prevented and treated, giving health authorities stronger scientific evidence to protect communities and reduce deaths during future outbreaks. 10 Tags: World Health Organization, Ebola Vaccine, Bundibugyo Virus, Democratic Republic of the Congo, Tumaini Clinical Trial, Oxford University, Moderna, Ring Vaccination, Ebola Treatment Research, Global Health Security POST / READ COMMENTS TRENDING 1 EIB-Led Alliance Lines Up Over €10 Billion to Help European Tech Firms Scale... The move marks an important step in efforts to develop vaccines against the Bundibugyo virus, which is responsible for the current Ebola outbreak. The recommendation also marks the first time that vaccines specifically developed to protect against the Bundibugyo virus will undergo evaluation during an active outbreak. Two New Vaccine Candidates Recommended The two vaccine candidates are ChAdOx1, developed by the University of Oxford in collaboration with the Serum Institute of India, and Moderna’s mRNA-1469. WHO’s independent Technical Advisory Group on Candidate Vaccine Prioritization recommended both candidates for further clinical evaluation based on available preclinical and early clinical evidence. The candidates will join the ongoing Tumaini trial once they receive the necessary national approvals. WHO Director-General Dr Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus highlighted the importance of scientific collaboration and clinical research in tackling the outbreak. He noted that the participation of researchers, healthcare workers and trial volunteers would help generate vital evidence to support future outbreak responses. Also Read | Russia Introduces World’s First Cell-Based Therapy for Eardrum Repair Tumaini Trial to Evaluate Multiple Vaccines The National Institute of Biomedical Research (INRB) in the DRC is leading the vaccine trial, with support from the University of Antwerp, WHO, Epicentre, Médecins Sans Frontières, the Institute of Tropical Medicine of Antwerp and the Africa Centres for Disease Control and Prevention. The Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI) has also supported the rapid development of the vaccine candidates through its investments. The Tumaini trial uses a ring-vaccination approach to evaluate multiple vaccine candidates within a single study. Under this approach, researchers vaccinate contacts of people with confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease to assess vaccine effectiveness. The trial builds on an approach used during the West Africa Ebola outbreak a decade ago. At that time, a landmark study in Guinea established the effectiveness of Ervebo against the Zaire ebolavirus. Ervebo is the first vaccine being evaluated in the Tumaini trial to assess its effectiveness against the Bundibugyo virus. So far, researchers have established four vaccination rings and are preparing several more. These rings include contacts of people who have fallen ill or died from the disease. Also Read | Doctors at Amor Hospitals Save Factory Worker After Near-Fatal Chemical Accident Ebola Treatment Research Also Progresses Alongside vaccine development, researchers are advancing clinical studies to identify potential treatments for Bundibugyo virus disease. The WHO-sponsored PARTNERS trial, launched in July, is evaluating whether the monoclonal antibody MBP134, the antiviral drug remdesivir or a combination of both can improve survival among patients with confirmed infections. Furthermore, researchers plan to add maftivimab to the trial to assess its potential as a treatment. A separate post-exposure prophylaxis study involving obeldevisir is also underway. WHO Supports Ebola Research and Clinical Studies WHO is supporting research activities through its R&D Blueprint and Health Emergencies Programme. Its efforts include developing research protocols, providing technical guidance, coordinating research partners and supporting the integration of ethical and scientifically rigorous studies into the outbreak response. Initial findings from the treatment trials are expected in the coming months, while results from the vaccine trial are anticipated in early 2027. As reported by the World Health Organization (WHO), the ongoing research aims to strengthen the scientific evidence available for preventing and treating Bundibugyo virus disease and improving responses to future Ebola outbreaks. supplementary_news.content: 10°C overcast clouds TFL Updates Search for: Search Search LDN Write For Us Login London News Lifestyle Entrepreneurship Fitness & Health Finance Tech Food & Drink Automotive Travel Global Ebola trial advisers back two Bundibugyo vaccine candidates By LDN Editor 05 November 2026 4 minute read Listen to this article Independent advisers have recommended adding two experimental vaccines designed specifically for the Bundibugyo virus to an Ebola study under way in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The World Health Organisation said the candidates, known as ChAdOx1 and mRNA-1469, could enter the Tumaini trial after national approvals. The recommendation is not itself a regulatory approval, and neither candidate has been shown to protect people against the virus in this outbreak. ChAdOx1 is being developed by the University of Oxford with the Serum Institute of India. The mRNA-1469 candidate is being developed by Moderna. An independent advisory group convened by the health organisation recommended both for further clinical evaluation after considering preclinical and early clinical evidence. The companies were informed on Monday, the organisation said in its announcement on Wednesday. It expects results from the vaccine trial in early 2027, although that is an expectation rather than a confirmed date for findings. A new stage for an existing study The recommendation follows the start of Tumaini in Bunia, in the country’s north-eastern Ituri province. The first participant was vaccinated on 23 October. The study is led by the Congolese National Institute for Biomedical Research and the University of Antwerp, with national and international partners. The two Bundibugyo-specific candidates had already been identified as possible additions to the study. The new development is the advisers’ recommendation that both be evaluated, subject to the required national approvals. It is not an announcement that vaccinations with either new candidate have already begun. Tumaini is a phase 2/3 trial designed to assess the safety, immune response and effectiveness of vaccine candidates. Its adaptive structure allows more than one candidate to be examined within the same study, rather than requiring a wholly separate trial for each one. The study uses a ring-vaccination approach, enrolling contacts of people with confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease. The World Health Organisation said four vaccination rings were already in place and several more were being prepared. The rings include contacts of people who became ill or died from Ebola. Ervebo is the first vaccine being evaluated in the study. It is licensed against Ebola virus, also known as Zaire ebolavirus, but was not designed specifically for Bundibugyo. Researchers are assessing whether it offers protection against the virus responsible for the current outbreak; that protection has not been established. The proposed additions address a different question: whether vaccines designed for Bundibugyo can safely protect people exposed to that virus. The health organisation said their evaluation would be the first time specifically designed candidates had been tested during an outbreak of the disease. Research alongside the response Bundibugyo is one of several viruses that can cause Ebola disease. There is no licensed vaccine specifically against it. The disease can spread through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person or contaminated materials, and early supportive care can improve a patient’s chance of survival. Finding a vaccine is only one part of the response. Health teams also work to identify infections, trace contacts, care for patients and support safe, dignified burials. Those measures continue while researchers gather evidence; the recommendation does not establish that transmission has stopped. A separate treatment study is assessing the antibody MBP134, the antiviral remdesivir and a combination of the two in patients with confirmed Bundibugyo virus disease. The health organisation said another antibody, maftivimab, would soon be added. These are investigations into treatment, not proof that the medicines work against Bundibugyo. For the vaccine candidates, the next steps are national approvals and their entry into the trial. The results will be needed to establish how well the products perform and whether they can offer a useful additional tool for future outbreak responses. Featured image: AI-generated illustration. supplementary_news.content: Home Animals Biology Environment Health & Medicine Tech Travel Space Natureworldnews.com Let's Connect Trending climate change Earth whales Ebola Cases Top 10,000 in Congo as Africa CDC Toll Shows More Than Half of Patients Have Died By Avery Porter Published: Nov 06 2026, 7:32 AM EST Facebook Twitter Linkedin Comment Mail Tony KARUMBA | AFP via Getty Images Developing Story Note: This report covers new developments involving the Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Information may change as health agencies release additional findings. CDC figures are data through Nov. 1, 2026, from a page updated Nov. 3. Africa CDC death figures were reported Nov. 2, 2026, with Congo data through Oct. 31. The Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has passed 10,000 confirmed cases, and Africa CDC's latest count shows more than half of infected people have died. Africa CDC reported 5,376 deaths as of Nov. 2, according to Al Jazeera, with about 10,444 infections across Congo, Uganda, and Kenya. The U.S. CDC's situation page, using confirmed cases only, lists 10,563 cases and 5,130 deaths through Nov. 1. By that measure, just under half of confirmed patients have died. Either way, the outbreak crossed two grim thresholds in the same week — and it is now among the deadliest Ebola epidemics on record. Two Agencies, Two Counts, One Trend The difference between the two tallies matters for readers trying to understand the numbers. CDC counts confirmed cases and confirmed deaths separately and excludes suspected cases pending investigation. Africa CDC's figures, given to reporters, were compiled on a different schedule. Neither agency explained the gap publicly, and the true fatality rate may shift as recent patients recover or die. What both counts show is a death rate far higher than many recent outbreaks. The World Health Organization says Ebola fatality has ranged from about 25% to 90% in past outbreaks. Euronews, citing AFP, described this as the fastest-growing and most widespread Ebola epidemic on record. Nature World News previously reported that cases were nearing 10,000 as Congo launched its first vaccine trial and the U.S. added a travel attestation. At that time, CDC data through Oct. 23 showed 9,847 cases and 4,761 deaths. In roughly nine days, about 700 more confirmed cases and nearly 370 more deaths were added. The Strain That Existing Shots Were Not Built For Bundibugyo is one of several viruses that cause Ebola disease, and it is rare. Before 2026, it had caused only two known outbreaks, in Uganda in 2007 and Congo in 2012, each with fewer than 60 cases. That rarity is the core problem — the vaccine and antibody treatments developed over the past decade target Zaire ebolavirus, the species behind the 2014 to 2016 West African epidemic. The Associated Press reports none is approved for Bundibugyo. Doctors in Congo are now testing whether Ervebo, the licensed Zaire vaccine, offers any cross-protection, with Bundibugyo-specific candidates expected to follow. No result from that trial has been published. Conflict compounds the medical gap. Eastern Congo has seen attacks on Ebola facilities and displacement, which slows contact tracing and keeps sick people from early care. Early in the outbreak, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus warned that responders were "playing catch-up" after delayed detection. Where the Virus Has Spread CDC lists confirmed cases in eight Congolese provinces: Bas-Uele, Haut-Uele, Ituri, Nord-Kivu, Sud-Kivu, Sud-Ubangi, Tshopo and Nord-Ubangi. Ituri, the original epicenter around Bunia, has carried the largest share. Beyond Congo, Uganda recorded 20 cases before its outbreak was declared over. Kenya confirmed its first-ever Ebola cases in October, nine in all with two deaths, all in Nairobi and all linked to the first patient. Kenya's health ministry has reported no community spread. Nigeria confirmed one imported case on Oct. 20 in Abuja. The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control said that the patient and a close contact were medically evacuated to Switzerland on Oct. 26. France treated one case in July, and that patient has recovered. Low Risk at Home, New Rules at the Airport For Americans, the official message is unchanged. "The overall risk to the American public and travelers remains low," the CDC states. CDC's case table lists no cases in the United States. What has changed is airport procedure. After 11:59 p.m. EST on Nov. 3, every passenger on an international flight to the United States must attest they have not been in Congo in the previous 21 days. Travelers who were in Congo within 21 days cannot board commercial flights to the U.S. U.S. citizens and nationals arriving from Uganda or South Sudan must enter through designated airports for enhanced screening. CDC's Level 4 notice tells Americans to avoid all travel to Ituri and Nord-Kivu provinces. It advises reconsidering nonessential travel to Haut-Uele and Tshopo, and enhanced precautions elsewhere in Congo and in Uganda. The people most affected by these rules are aid workers, health care staff, missionaries, business travelers and families with relatives in the region. Anyone with recent travel to an affected area who develops fever, severe headache, muscle pain, vomiting, diarrhea or unexplained bleeding within 21 days should call a doctor or health department before arriving at a clinic, so staff can prepare. Ebola spreads through direct contact with the blood or body fluids of a sick person, not through casual contact or the air. Several important questions remain unanswered. It is not yet known whether Ervebo protects against Bundibugyo, whether the Kenya and Nigeria clusters are fully contained, or whether cases in Ituri are truly declining. The next data points to watch are CDC's weekly situation updates, WHO's Disease Outbreak News reports, and early findings from the vaccine trial. The milestone is grim, and the outbreak is not under control. Still, the danger remains concentrated in eastern Congo and among people with direct exposure. For U.S. readers, the practical step is limited to travel awareness and early reporting of symptoms after time in affected areas. CDC lists 10,532 confirmed cases in Congo and 10,563 across all affected countries, with data through Nov. 1, 2026. Is the death rate really above 50%? Africa CDC's count puts deaths slightly above half of infections. CDC's confirmed-only count is just under half. The rate may change as recent cases resolve. Why is Bundibugyo harder to fight? Approved Ebola vaccines and antibody treatments target a different species, Zaire ebolavirus. None is approved for Bundibugyo. Which countries have reported cases? Congo, Uganda, Kenya, Nigeria, and France. Uganda and France have no active cases. What is the risk to Americans? CDC says the overall risk to the American public and travelers remains low. What changed for U.S.-bound travelers? supplementary_news.content: Skip to main content Edition: ENInternational Edition Kosovo Albania International Deutsch Health Where is the British doctor with Ebola being treated? A London isolation unit, and the public risk is low A British doctor who caught Ebola in DR Congo is in the Royal Free Hospital's high-level isolation unit in London. UKHSA says the risk to the wider public remains low. By Nacionale News · November 6, 2026, 5:32 a.m. ET4 min read Photo: Matt Brown / Wikimedia Commons · CC BY 2.0 The British doctor who caught Ebola in the Democratic Republic of the Congo is being treated in the high-level isolation unit at the Royal Free Hospital in London, and the UK Health Security Agency says the risk to the wider public remains low, according to the Department of Health and Social Care. Ebola does not spread through the air: it passes through direct contact with the bodily fluids of someone who has symptoms. The doctor’s name, condition and how they were exposed have not been released. So yes, there is now one confirmed Ebola patient in the UK. The patient is in a sealed unit built for this purpose, and the NHS says Ebola has never been spread from person to person in the UK. What happened The doctor had been working on the Ebola epidemic in DR Congo and tested positive there. The UK and DRC governments and international health partners arranged a medical evacuation flight, and the patient arrived on Thursday 5 November, according to the government statement and the Associated Press. The government says the flight followed established infection prevention and control procedures, which also cover everyone involved in the patient’s care. The AP reports that this is the first British patient evacuated from the current outbreak and the third person with a positive test to be returned to Europe. A doctor in France who fell ill after a humanitarian mission in Congo was confirmed in June and has since recovered, the AP says. What UKHSA and the NHS say about the risk Dr Renu Bindra, deputy director of UKHSA’s All Hazards Public Health Response, said the risk to the wider public “remains low”, in the government statement. She told the AP that “robust infection prevention and control protocols are in place”. According to the government, the Royal Free unit has strict protocols so the patient has no contact with members of the public, and staff wear protective equipment and follow other measures to stop transmission. The NHS Ebola page also describes the risk to people in the UK as low. Inside the Royal Free isolation unit The Royal Free in Hampstead, north London, has a high-level isolation unit run by a dedicated team of doctors, nurses and laboratory staff. It has treated patients with Lassa fever, Ebola and Crimean-Congo haemorrhagic fever before, LBC reports. Access is restricted, staff care for the patient through a special tent with controlled ventilation, and all air leaving the unit is cleaned, according to LBC. The unit also treated patients during the 2014 to 2015 West Africa outbreak, the AP notes. In March 2015, for example, a UK military healthcare worker diagnosed in Sierra Leone was flown to the Royal Free, according to a government release from the time. Before this case, only four confirmed Ebola cases had been recorded in the UK: one in 1976 after a needle incident in a laboratory, and three health workers during the West Africa outbreak, LBC reports. How Ebola spreads, and how it does not It spreads through contact with the body fluids of an infected person or wild animal, such as blood, vomit, saliva and urine (NHS). It does not spread through the air (DHSC and UKHSA). People are generally not infectious until they develop symptoms, Dr Damien Tully of the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine told LBC. Symptoms can appear 2 to 21 days after infection. They often start suddenly, like flu, with fever, extreme tiredness and headache, and can later include vomiting, diarrhoea, rash and bleeding or bruising (NHS). Tully called the infection “deeply concerning, but it is not entirely unexpected”, according to the AP, because health workers can be exposed by accident even with careful protection. He told LBC the case does not suggest the virus has become more transmissible. The outbreak in DR Congo The outbreak is caused by Bundibugyo virus, one of the Ebola viruses. As of 4 November, DR Congo had reported 10,668 confirmed cases and 5,198 related deaths across eight provinces, according to the European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control. The AP says it has spread to 67 health zones, from three when it was declared in May. Other patients from the outbreak have been evacuated to Switzerland and the Netherlands, the ECDC reports. What to do if you are worried The NHS says to call NHS 111 if you have travelled to an affected country and have symptoms, or have been in contact with a traveller who has symptoms. Stay at home and avoid close contact with others until you are told what to do. Contact with the general public is not a concern in this case: the patient travelled on a medical evacuation flight and went straight into isolation, according to the government. What we don’t know The doctor’s name, age and current condition have not been released. How and when the doctor was exposed in DR Congo has not been made public. Officials have not said what treatment the doctor is receiving. No official statement has said whether anyone else who worked with the doctor is being monitored. Read more Is Ebola in the UK? Tropical Medicine London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine https://lshtm.ac.uk/themes/custom/lshtm/images/lshtm-logo-black.png Share LSHTM expert says the risk from planned medical evacuation is low and incident does not suggest UK public is at increased risk Illustration of Ebola virus showing long thin curving light blue filament with two loops and wing-like structure on lefthand side and righthand end curving upwards against dark blue background The UK government has confirmed that a British man who has tested positive for Ebola in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has been flown back to the UK in a planned medical evacuation. It is the first case involving a British national contracting Ebola linked to the ongoing outbreak centred on DRC caused by Bundibugyo virus. So far the outbreak has led to over 5,000 deaths. The man, who is a medical doctor, was infected while working for a humanitarian organisation as part of the response to the outbreak. He was transported to the Royal Free Hospital, London, on 5 November 2026. Dr Damien Tully, Associate Professor at the Medical Research Council/Uganda Virus Research Institute and London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine (MRC/UVRI and LSHTM) Uganda Research Unit said: “The infection of a British healthcare worker with Ebola is deeply concerning, but it is not entirely unexpected. Healthcare workers are on the frontline of these outbreaks, often treating severely ill patients under extremely challenging conditions. Even with rigorous protective measures, accidental exposures can occur. "This case is a stark reminder of the risks faced by those responding to the outbreak of Ebola disease caused by Bundibugyo virus in the DRC. However, it does not suggest that the virus has become more transmissible or that the threat to the UK has increased. “Unlike respiratory viruses such as COVID-19 and influenza, that can spread through the air, Ebola is transmitted primarily through direct contact with infected bodily fluids, and people are not generally infectious until they develop symptoms. This means that identifying and isolating cases, together with appropriate infection prevention measures, can be highly effective in preventing onward transmission. For the UK public, the risk from this planned medical evacuation is extremely low. “The UK has well-established procedures for managing cases of viral haemorrhagic fever, including two dedicated high-level isolation units at the Royal Free Hospital in London and the Royal Victoria Infirmary in Newcastle. These facilities are equipped with specialist isolation systems and staffed by highly trained infectious disease teams. Patients can be transported under carefully controlled conditions, with strict infection prevention measures, appropriate protective equipment and arrangements for identifying and monitoring anyone who may have been exposed. “Crucially, a planned medical evacuation such as this allows established protocols within the NHS England specialist infectious disease network to be activated in advance, ensuring that healthcare teams, transport arrangements and isolation facilities are coordinated before the patient arrives. These measures substantially reduce the risk of onward transmission to healthcare workers and the wider public. “The UK has been here before. During the 2014–2016 West African Ebola epidemic, three infected healthcare workers were treated in the UK, including two who were medically evacuated from Sierra Leone. All three recovered, with no onward transmission in the UK. This experience provides reassurance that specialist isolation facilities and established infection prevention procedures can successfully manage patients infected overseas while minimising the risk of onward transmission. "While this case is understandably attracting attention in the UK, the greatest danger remains in the communities affected by the outbreak in the DRC and elsewhere in the region. Protecting frontline healthcare workers, rapidly identifying and isolating cases, and interrupting transmission at its source remain critical to preventing further infections and international spread.” This is a rapid reaction to a breaking news story. This story was updated on 5 November 2026 to reflect that the man had been transported to the Royal Free Hospital, London and on 6 November 2026 to confirm the man is a medical doctor. supplementary_news.content: MSF DRC EBOLA: MSF calls for broader access to ERVEBO® vaccine during Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak 9 November - As the Bundibugyo Ebola outbreak continues in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC), Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) is calling for rapid expansion of access to ERVEBO®, the only Ebola vaccine currently available at scale. While vaccines specifically developed against the Bundibugyo virus are still under development and unlikely to be available in the near term, growing evidence and encouraging field observations suggest that ERVEBO® could help protect more people at risk today. 09/11/2026 Latest stories MSF WEST BANK: Flashquote on lockdown imposed by Israeli force Federica Venturi, Project Coordinator for Hebron, MSF Palestine: 06/11/2026 MSF Yemen: Urgent action needed to stop spread of acute watery diarrhoea in Hajjah governate 04/11/2026 MSF MYANMAR: Deadly airstrike damages maternity ward in Mrauk-U, Rakhine State, killing five including a newborn 3 November 2026 - Paul Brockmann, MSF Operations Manager said: “We are horrified by Sunday’s airstrike which damaged the temporary maternity ward in Mrauk-U. We have received reports that five civilians — including a newborn — were killed in the bombing with more wounded. The death of the newborn is especially heartbreaking and underscores the utterly unacceptable toll these attacks take on the most vulnerable. Hospitals and patients must never be put at such risk. This attack follows a previous deadly strike on the Mrauk-U hospital in December 2025. Enough is enough. Even war has rules: children, civilians and healthcare workers throughout conflict-affected Rakhine need protection and services, not repeated attacks.” 03/11/2026 MSF GAZA: MSF surgeon must be released after two years of arbitrary detention Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) calls for the immediate and unconditional release of Dr Mohammed Obeid. He remains detained by Israel without any charges since 26 October 2024. 02/11/2026 MSF HAITI: MSF supports health services amid violence in Artibonite region 6 November - Haiti is in the midst of a humanitarian crisis amid conflict between armed groups and the government and its allies. Beyond the capital, Port-au-Prince, the towns and rural communities of the lower Artibonite region are among the hardest hit. 06/11/2026 MSF DRC: Harmful, restrictive measures obstruct care for sexual violence survivors 02/11/2026 - Goma, Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC): The de facto authorities in North Kivu province, eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) – the FRN1, formerly AFC/M23 – have been imposing harmful restrictions related to seeking care for sexual violence for months. These policies obstruct people from accessing this essential care and put them at greater risk, says Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF). Following a commitment made to MSF in early October 2026, we urge the de facto authorities to immediately stop these measures and guarantee safe, confidential access to care. 04/11/2026 MSF COP31: World leaders must urgently step up climate action to protect health COP31 must put health at the centre of climate action, turning negotiations and declarations into concrete action for the world’s most affected communities, says Médecins Sans Frontières/Doctors Without Borders (MSF). 03/11/2026 MSF Gaza: Israeli restrictions put an end to 3D masks for children with burns 29/10/2026 MSF Ukraine: Teams evacuate patients from hospital damaged in Russian attack on Dnipro 04/11/2026 MSF SOUTH SUDAN: Funding cuts: The Human Cost of Disinvestment 3 November - Every day in Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF)-supported secondary hospitals across South Sudan, from Aweil, in a stable area under government control, to Akobo in Jonglei, an unstable conflict zone held by opposition groups, our teams receive women and children in increasingly severe condition, dying from diseases that could have been diagnosed and treated weeks earlier. Across the country, thousands of mothers and children find the doors of their primary healthcare clinics shuttered. They must travel long distances, at a cost they cannot afford, to reach a hospital only after preventable conditions have become critical. 03/11/2026 MSF Ukraine: Temporary ceasefire enables MSF to deliver medicines to Kherson villages near frontline 02/11/2026 MSF Haiti: Teams warn of a surge in violence in Port-au-Prince and urge protection of civilians 28/10/2026 Contact us Hannah Hoexter Senior Press Officer - NEWS, MSF UK hannah.hoexter@london.msf.org (44) 7342 662 441 Emma Dixon Head of Media, MSF emma.dixon@london.msf.org +44 207 067 4236 David Whitty press officer, MSF david.whitty@london.msf.org +44 (0)207-067-4236 msf.org.uk/ Kate Lee katriona.lee@london.msf.org Cece Leadon cece.leadon@london.msf.org +44 (0) 207 067 4236 Heba Yousef MSF UK heba.yousef@london.msf.org 07999330856 MSF UK media@london.msf.org +44 (0) 207 067 4236

supplementary_news.content: Latest News Syria Middle East Economy Politics Sport International Reading: WHO recommends two new vaccine candidates for Ebola trials AR TR FR ES KU Latest News Syria Middle East Economy Politics Sport International Reading: WHO recommends two new vaccine candidates for Ebola trials AR TR FR ES KU Culture Video Photos Miscellaneous Latest News Syria Middle East Economy Politics Sport International Search Latest News News Categories Politics Culture Video Photos Miscellaneous Provinces Languages العربية Türkçe Français Español Kurdî Follow US WHO recommends two new vaccine candidates for Ebola trials Published: 2026/11/05 10:57 AM Updated: 2026/11/05 10:59 AM World Health Organization (WHO) Logo – Geneva Geneva, Nov. 5 (SANA) The World Health Organization (WHO) has recommended adding two experimental vaccine candidates to clinical trials targeting the Bundibugyo virus, amid the ongoing outbreak in Africa, particularly in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC), where the death toll has exceeded 5,300. In a statement published on its website on Wednesday, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said the organization’s expert groups had recommended including the two candidates in trials that began last month using the Ervebo vaccine. Ervebo is approved for protection against Ebola virus disease but is not approved for the Bundibugyo virus currently spreading in the DRC. The two candidates are ChAdOx1 BDBV, developed by the University of Oxford in cooperation with India’s Serum Institute, and mRNA-1469, developed by Moderna. Both are designed to target the Bundibugyo virus, Ghebreyesus said. On Nov. 2, Ghebreyesus said the outbreak in the DRC underscored the urgent need to finalize the international agreement on pandemics and strengthen cooperation among countries to address health threats that cross borders.
